items.title: 673: Nvidia Without Jensen Huang, GPT-6.2 Backlash, Two Questions for Anthropic’s IPO, OpenAI + NATO, a Sky Full of Satellites, Dyson’s $10 Fix, and Lord of the Rings
items.body: Passing one obstacle simply says you’re worthy of more. —Ryan Holiday 🛰️🌐 This is going on above your head at all times. Photographer Brendan Larsen created this amazing composite: This is the most time-consuming photo edit I’ve EVER done! I left my camera photographing the night sky over Mt Taranaki for nearly TWO HOURS, capturing 578 photographs. The result? An estimated 14,450 satellite trail appearances, representing approximately 1,400 individual satellites! 😱 I manually masked in EVERY SINGLE TRAIL from the original photographs — approximately 45 HOURS of editing to create this one image! h/t Friend-of-the-show and supporter DvorakQ (💚 🥃) on the private discord! ⚙️🛠️🧰 Pro-tip for you: If you have a Dyson cordless vacuum, maybe because you bought one after hearing David Senra’s (🎙️📚) episode about James Dyson in 2021, and you’ve had it for a number of years, buy a new one of these: You can get non-Dyson ones on Amazon for less than half the price of the original one. Maybe I didn’t read the instructions closely enough, but I thought these filters just needed to be washed with water once in a while. Turns out, they are consumable 😅 My V15 was starting to have problems. I suspected the hardwood brush (the yellow and blue one that spins), because when I plugged it in, I got the “airways blocked” warning, but I didn’t get it with other attachments. I was about to spend 150 CAD on a new brush, but on a hunch, I decided to order a new filter. Holy! It’s like I got a brand new vacuum. It sucks so much — in a good way 😅 — that I feel it pulling against carpets and floorboards in a way that I haven’t felt in years. Performance had been degrading so gradually that I never noticed the problem. I’m glad I spent ~10 CAD on a filter rather than more on an attachment that wouldn’t have solved the problem, and then maybe I would’ve just bought a whole new V15 for a thousand bucks. I figure this is a good enough tip to share with you. 💚 🥃 To keep this steamboat alive and afloat , I need supporters. Like you ! 🚢 The paid subscription includes the full feed, every podcast, Zoom Q&As with me, and access to the private Discord clubhouse , where a core group of us hang out and discuss the interesting stuff we find: Get the full Liberty feed and help keep the Serendipity Engine running by becoming a paid supporter. Thank you 💚🥃🦊🐙⚓️ 🏦 💰 Liberty Capital 💳 💴 🏎️ Fall From Grace: The World Changed Faster Than Jensen Did 🪽 I have written and rewritten thousands of words on this since last week. Events happened so fast that right after I published my Oh, Jensen piece, it was rapidly obsolete because he resigned and two other affairs came to light. Who knows what else will happen by the time you are reading this ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ I could tell you a lot of things. My mind is like Schrödinger’s cat when it comes to this. I’m both extremely disappointed in Jensen for his behavior and failings, and disappointed that he resigned and the trajectory of world history will be different because of it (right, I mean, if you think about how much leverage this powerful tech has on *everything*). I’m sure you’ve followed the coverage and commentary. It’s been hard to avoid. So I won’t recap all the facts and arguments. Instead, I’ll tell you my read on the situation, and I think Ben Thompson (💚 🥃 🎩) nailed it when he wrote : Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted. It’s hard to remember how fast everything happened, because it simultaneously feels fast and long. How long ago was the ancient GPT-4o? Remember how much of a splash that made? That’s 2.5 years ago. Or o1? Remember the big 🍓 brouhaha? That was about two years ago. Decades happened in the past three years, it seems like. Some things can go fast, but some things take time. Not long ago, Nvidia was basically a video game company that cared immensely about the latest Call of Duty or Cyberpunk 2077 releases (🎮). They went from floating on a side island in the tech world (they were rarely mentioned along with the rest of Big Tech) to central to EVERYTHING in basically no time. Google and Microsoft and Amazon had many years to figure out how to be big. How to deal with politicians and their role in geopolitics. And even with all that extra time, they each had their own struggles and moments of crisis. Jensen was thrown into it, and it’s not like he wasn’t also busy with the tech side of things. But on the side, he became a global rockstar and power broker, reshaping industries with his decisions and shifting the balance of power between countries with his chips. That’s got to make your head spin. 😵‍💫 Not to excuse, but maybe to explain . Maybe Jensen spent his whole career driving like a Formula 1 racer. He was incredibly good at it. But somewhere along the way, the closed circuit racetrack became a public highway, and he was still driving the same way. 🏎️ Jensen had extraordinary foresight about tech. What about everything else? Maybe the qualities that made him so incredibly effective as a founder and tech CEO were the same that contributed to his downfall ( your strengths are your weaknesses ). The whole ‘ 60-direct reports 1 , F1 car finely tuned to be driven by Jensen ’ thing made them operate at startup speed and leverage Jensen’s own talent in a way that it may have been diluted in a company with more process and bureaucracy. But it also meant that so much was going through him. It was built to take maximum advantage of his strengths, which means it became highly dependent on his judgement as the flip side of that coin. What happens when that judgement fails? 😬 Just yesterday, Nvidia announced a board-level committee to oversee national-security and export-control compliance. Was he prioritizing Nvidia’s commercial success (as a founder who has the scars of multiple near-bankruptcies would) even as some powerful national-security officials increasingly expected the company to play ball and be a centerpiece of their national-security strategy against China? You can agree or disagree with his arguments for selling older/hobbled chips to China, but it’s possible that those who disagreed with him used what they knew about him to get him out of their way. We don’t know who leaked what, or why, but there’s clearly been a power struggle in Washington, and Jensen being gone was a big win for those pushing for tighter restrictions. What will happen next? ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ The camps are clear. Many shareholders and players in the tech industry are pushing for him to come back, while others in positions of power (including Treasury Secretary Bessent) clearly want him to stay away. Jensen has said he’s open to return , but it’s just one of the many preconditions required. On the earnings call yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said that the board doesn’t intend to bring him back . We don’t know if more revelations will come out and reshuffle the deck or if the board will be convinced there’s a path somehow… This isn’t over. I’ll leave you on Tobi Lütke on Jensen (and donating blood to three hospitals to be able to buy a Riva TNT GPU 🩸): 📊 Two Questions Going into Anthropic’s IPO 🤔 There are a lot of questions to ask about Anthropic as a business going into its IPO, but two keep coming back to me. I don’t know the answers, but sometimes the questions are what matters most, and over time, as we watch things closely, maybe we’ll find answers. 1. Is Anthropic becoming a platform businesses build around or a supplier they can swap out? 🕸️ I’m sure you’ve seen the line from Anthropic’s S-1 about how over 80% of its Q3 revenue came from models released in the preceding six months. There are a couple of ways to interpret that. 🔀 One is that these things have a very short half-life and there’s very little loyalty to a model and users will just go to what’s best for them. But another possibility is that Anthropic is replacing its own models without losing its customers . Even if any particular model’s advantage only lasts a few months, customers may keep moving to the next Claude because they trust Anthropic to stay competitive. Model-version turnover is not customer churn. 🔄 What I’m curious about is what happens when another lab has a clear lead for a while. Do Anthropic’s customers jump ship, or do they stick around waiting for the next Claude because they trust Anthropic to catch up quickly, so it’s not worth switching? 2. How much of Anthropic’s research spending buys growth and how much is to keep it competitive? 💰 🤷‍♂️ 💸 Serving inference may be super profitable, but what does it cost to keep making the models that customers want to buy? The numbers give us some idea of the scale. According to Anthropic's S-1 (which got an update yesterday to reveal the size of Google and Amazon’s stakes: 13.7% and 14.7% respectively), in the first nine months of 2026, it generated $33.2 billion in revenue with $4.8 billion in cost of revenue (mostly compute to serve customers). But it also had $19.2 billion in R&D expenses , including compute for developing models, research, internal usage, and personnel. Are they spending so much to press their advantage because they believe this will become a winner-take-all or duopoly market? Or are they spending that much because they have to, just to avoid falling behind OpenAI, Meta, Google, etc.? Of course, I suspect it’s not binary and there’s some of both, but the proportions can make a BIG difference to the economics of the business. If even the cheaper, non-frontier models can do most things, why would anyone keep paying a premium for the very best? Maybe because mistakes can be expensive. 💣⚠️💥 If using a cheaper model means spending hours checking and fixing its work, or risking lost revenue because something went wrong, paying more for some overkill model could actually be the cheaper option overall. So maybe the frontier will remain worth paying for even when the models a generation or two behind it are incredibly capable. From the full feed 🔒: The AI Boom Meets Its Political Bottleneck 🧪🔬 Liberty Labs 🧬 🔭 🏴‍☠️🔐 Alex Stamos: AI is Breaking Cybersecurity, So Why Not Rebuild Linux? Alex Stamos is someone worth listening to when it comes to cybersecurity. He spent decades in the field. He was the top security executive at Yahoo and Facebook (you may have heard his name because he helped investigate Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election), he founded the Stanford Internet Observatory, and teaches cybersecurity at Stanford. He's now chief security officer at Cognition, the AI coding company. He’s on the frontlines. He recently spoke with Nilay Patel on Decoder and I really enjoyed the interview. Here are some highlights: - 💰 The Economics of Cybersecurity Are Breaking Alex Stamos: We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense . You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high . It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. I think that is critical. That’s something I am personally extremely focused on. To be frank, very few people are. […] But for those models, we need to do a lot more work to optimize them and we need to make them cheap. I have a colleague who works at one of the large security platform companies who said that doing an investigation on one of the big frontier model cyber models costs $900 on their product to do an investigation. That is not going to work when the Russian ransomware guys are either using Macs or they’re using throwaway crypto mining rigs and their marginal cost is zero. At the end of the day, Economics 101 rules everything. There’s an asymmetry between attackers and defenders . Attackers don’t need a high success rate, they just need to find one weakness they can exploit. Defenders have to protect against many different kinds of attacks, detect the ones that get through, and contain the damage. -🐧🤖 Google and Amazon Should Rewrite Linux in Rust That was my favorite part of the interview and I’d love to see that actually happen. Alex Stamos: If you’re looking at your code base and you scan it and you’ve got 10,000 bugs, then probably now we are at the point where rewriting it is actually cheaper. […] I wish […] Google would take all of those incredibly brilliant engineers and just tell them, “Take the Linux kernel and rewrite this in Rust.” That would be their gift to the world. […] And then just release it and call it whatever you want, the G Linux kernel, just like they did this with OpenSSL. And I would run that. Cognition would run that on our servers or have Google and Amazon do it together and it would cost them $100 million , but compared to the societal cost that this is costing us every time we have to patch the Linux kernel and you have to reboot every Linux machine on the entire planet, that’s what has to happen. Nilay Patel: I don’t think anyone’s in that position. I don’t think Linus Torvalds is in that position. Alex Stamos: No, I think Sundar Pichai and Andy Jassy are. But the good thing is that a huge number of the really important uses of Linux kernel are production server hardware. So fork it. Linus will never do it because Linus wants to support all that stuff and he’s got all these politics, but Google and Amazon don’t have to care about Linus Torvalds. I like these big ambitious ideas. I mean, coding models are now so good, and if they’re not good enough now, what about in six months or a year? We should seriously consider rewriting some of the central pieces of infrastructure that everything else depends on, using safer languages like Rust. It’s a little like the classic XKCD: We now have the tools to make a much more stable base to that block tower. Stamos isn’t proposing that Google and Amazon support every obscure piece of hardware ever made, either. His idea is to focus on the production server hardware they actually use, while keeping compatibility with the software running above the kernel. Even if it costs a billion dollars, or several billion, it could be a fantastic investment if it significantly reduces the security problems and maintenance burden of one of the most important pieces of infrastructure in the world. 💾 🛡️🤖 🌐 OpenAI + NATO OpenAI announced that NATO is already using its advanced cybersecurity models through Daybreak to find vulnerabilities, investigate suspicious activity, and help develop and test fixes. Usage has reached up to 300 billion tokens per month (inputs + outputs — which sounds like a lot, but now that I think of it, my own Codex use is a few tens of billions of tokens, so I guess it’s not that much 🤔). Maybe they’re counting differently or that number isn’t right. Anyway, that’s being put to work defending critical infrastructure. OpenAI also says that ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, used its models to identify four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, and all four have been patched . WSJ : As geopolitical tensions remain elevated, the alliance is grappling with increasingly sophisticated threats, particularly in cyberspace: a cyberattack recently targeted European supermarket refrigerators and freezers, causing tens of millions of dollars in damage from spoiled food and equipment failures. Hey, I wrote about that ! This is also being deployed in Ukraine to harden against Russian cyberattacks: The company said in September that Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation would use Daybreak to protect civilian infrastructure, providing access to tools to identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly. 👎👎 Are GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra Duds? 🤔 The model roulette can be a frustrating game. You may love a model version, but that doesn’t mean the next one will be anything like it. It’s a good reminder of how much of these LLMs are still black box, more ‘grown’ than designed. Sometimes you get the recipe just right and it tastes wonderful (like Opus 4.6, which was loved for its creativity, conversational intelligence, and personality, or Opus 5.5, which is a reliable workhorse). But sometimes, for whatever reason, it doesn’t come together, and you get models that people don’t like (even if the benchmark numbers are impressive… or on the other side of the ledge, Opus 5 and 4.7. OpenAI has its own equivalents of this, with GPT-5.6 Sol on one side and GPT-5 on the other). This is pure speculation, but with Anthropic’s IPO coming, and the recent release of Fable 5.2, OpenAI probably had a lot of pressure to come out with something. Maybe it wasn’t quite fully baked yet, but they released GPT 6.2 Sol and Astra, and so far the reaction from most of those with early access has been…. Not great, Bob So normally I would tell you more about how the model has improved on certain benchmarks and how its architecture is different or whatever. But today the most notable news is really the vibes. Matt ended changing his mind and posting this VERY negative review: I haven’t had enough time with them to have a real opinion yet, so stay tuned for my review. Tibo at OpenAI said that many of these reviews were done some days ago, and that they’ve since improved the model (probably by tweaking the system prompts). I don’t know how much they can do with just that. They may have to rush out 6.3 if they can make it better on those aspects… But at this time, 6.2 certainly appears to be a gift for Anthropic’s IPO. From the full feed 🔒: Microsoft and AI-Assisted ASIC Design 🎨 🎭 Liberty Studio 👩‍🎨 🎥 ⚔️🛡️ Watching the Lord of the Rings Trilogy with my Kids 🏰 I thought I would have to wait longer to watch these films with my kids, but I’ve learned a lot about what they can handle and can’t handle in recent times as we’ve watched all kinds of other films, and I decided they were ready. We watched the extended editions, which add up to 11h23mins (!!). It was more like watching a TV series than films, watching an hour at a time over a few weeks. They loved it. They had never seen anything quite that epic, and at various points I could see them get so carried away and excited that they would almost vibrate on the couch next to me. It was beautiful to see. For my part, I’m not the kind of nerd who re-watches these films often. I had seen all of them in theater when they came out. When I saw Fellowship, I had not read the books, so it kind of blew my mind. Then, I read the trilogy before seeing Two Towers and I remember being slightly disappointed by it. I enjoyed it, but when the books are fresh in your memory, it’s harder to appreciate the films for what they are. And somehow I had forgotten large parts of Return of the King . I didn’t remember the falling skulls and the Green Ghost Army and all that stuff. The films held up pretty well. Some of the effects have aged a little bit. I remember when I first saw Gollum, I thought he looked incredible. So photorealistic! And now when I look at him, he looks more like a video game character at times. Good thing that the performance by Andy Serkis is so good that it makes you forget about that, even today. We’ve come a long way with how we integrate 3D characters into scenes with subtle light effects and ray tracing and all that. It almost makes me wish there could be a remastered version where everything would be kept the same but some of the effects would be improved. I know this doesn’t always have a great track record (*cough* George Lucas), but maybe it could work here. 🤔 1 Btw, this phrase about 60 direct reports has been said so often that I rarely even take the time to think about it. But sixty people, each with a whole multi-thousand group of people around them working on very complex things (chips, supply chain, partnerships, software, R&D, financial deals, global compliance, etc). That’s a lot of people and that’s a lot of complex things to deal with on a daily basis.

items.title: Digital Advertising Industry Snapshot 3Q’26
items.body:
As I do after every quarter, let me share the snapshot of the overall digital advertising industry.

As a reminder, the actual digital advertising industry is larger than what my snapshot below shows, but this snapshot helps me gauge the broader digital advertising industry’s big picture. TikTok and Walmart advertising are notably missing here. Well, TikTok is a private company and Walmart doesn’t disclose their advertising revenue consistently.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!btvD!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F21618841-686d-4959-8191-f888e1943159_1365x1381.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!btvD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F21618841-686d-4959-8191-f888e1943159_1365x1381.png)

Sources: Company filings, [Daloopa](https://daloopa.com/?utm_source=MBI&utm_medium=Organic&utm_campaign=SourceLink), MBI estimates

**Some key takeaways from 3Q’26:**

Digital advertising industry **decelerated** from 20.2% in 2Q’26 to 16.1% in 3Q’26. As mentioned in my last quarter’s snapshot, given the tough comp I expected both Q3 and Q4 to experience deceleration.

Meta’s incremental share **jumped to 52.7%**. Outside the ATT-distorted 2022 numbers, this is the first time in this snapshot that Meta captured more than half of the incremental dollar. There is a bit of an asterisk here. Amazon moved Prime Day into June this year, so its ad growth slowed from 26% in 2Q’26 to 11% in 3Q’26, which mechanically flatters everyone else’s incremental share. **If I combine 2Q and 3Q, Meta’s incremental share was ~48%.** That is still comfortably ahead of its ~35% current share, so the share gain story remains fully intact even after adjusting for the Prime Day timing.

Google Search’s incremental share **dropped to 27.6%**, the lowest since 2Q’23 (which was again distorted by ATT). Last quarter I **[wondered](https://mbideepdives.substack.com/p/digital-advertising-industry-snapshot-921?utm_source=publication-search)** whether Search could hold ~30% incremental share or would drift toward the mid-20s. But we need to adjust for the Prime Day impact here as well. On a combined 2Q and 3Q basis, Search’s incremental share was just a tad bit below 30%. Let’s wait a couple more quarters to see if Google Search can stay around this level or keep drifting downwards.

Among the sub-scaled players, AppLovin and Reddit are still punching above their weight, with incremental shares of 3.2% and 1.2% against current shares of 1.2% and 0.5% respectively. AppLovin’s growth actually reaccelerated to 56%. Trade Desk’s revenue declined YoY for the first time in this snapshot, and its incremental share is now essentially zero. Snap (0.2% incremental share vs 0.8% current share) continues to lose relevance.

I should, however, note that some of the definitions of advertising here are not quite apple to apple as some companies report advertising dollar on a gross and some report on a net basis which is why I like to focus more on incremental share data.

I would also like to explain some changes for this quarter’s edition.

Digital advertising industry is defined as Alphabet’s advertising revenue+ Meta’s advertising revenue+ Snap’s ad revenue+ Pinterest revenue+ Microsoft Search and advertising revenue+ Amazon advertising revenue+ Trade Desk revenue+ AppLovin revenue+ Reddit’s ad revenue. Microsoft no longer discloses search advertising on its own, so I now use its “Search and advertising” line, which also includes LinkedIn’s ad and Premium subscription revenue. Microsoft restated this line back to 3Q’24, which is why its share steps up from ~2.7% to ~4% in that quarter. All the growth and incremental share numbers compare each quarter with the prior year on the same basis, so Microsoft gets no credit for the definition change. I also replaced Snap’s 2023 total revenue with estimated ad revenue. For 2022, I still assume Snap’s total revenue as their ad revenue, which is perhaps closer to reality anyway. Reddit’s number has only been included since 1Q’23 since we don’t have their ad revenue numbers in earlier years. Keep these in mind while looking at YoY comparisons in the past. Also note that for visual convenience, I have shaded all the Q3 of the last five years.

_Subscribers get the daily journal and five+ years of Deep Dives, i.e. full-length analyses with financial models on **[70](https://mbideepdives.substack.com/p/deep-dives)+** companies. The daily is just how I think out loud between the Deep Dives!_

**Current Portfolio:**

Please note that these are **NOT** my recommendation to buy/sell these securities, but just disclosure from my end so that you can assess potential biases that I may have because of my own personal portfolio holdings. Always consider my write-up my personal investing journal and never forget my objectives, risk tolerance, and constraints may have no resemblance to yours.

items.title: [AINews] GPT-6.2 Astra, the #2 Frontier Model is better and 20%-600% cheaper, but has mixed reviews; 6.2 Sol likely main workhorse
items.body: OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol today, two days before Anthropic’s expected first trading day . In Artificial Analysis ’ tests, Sol ties September’s Astra at about 15% of the cost per task . New Astra scores 62 on the Intelligence Index, just behind Fable 5.2 at 65. Net net, Anthropic still owns the world’s best model, but OpenAI owns the world’s most efficient models in terms of intelligence per $. What’s more unusual about this launch is the STRONGLY negative influencer feedback… which prompted a defensive response … View post on X ↗ We think that some of this is overreacting and normal influencer tendency to either have everything be 🤯🤯🤯 or the literal WORST.MODEL.EVER, BUT also that some of the criticisms are valid, and the RL artefacts are noticeable and downright bizarre (don’t even get us started about the terrible launch video ). However, we still use it to automate our work and that’s all that matters in the end. Great ship, but Anthropic’s IPO is unaffected and that will be probably the headline of the week/year/decade (until OpenAI IPO’s….) Today’s AI News is brought to you by SerpApi! Check them out to support LS, and contact business@latent.space for feedback! AI Twitter Recap GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Availability. Astra is $8 input, $0.40 cached input and $40 output. Sol keeps its predecessor’s pricing at $2, $0.10 and $10. Both have 1M context and a 128K output limit. Vals · Ultrafast pricing and rollout Astra for Law. The Enterprise configuration adds a legal search index. Artificial Analysis measured 20.8% on Harvey LAB-AA, versus 15.0% for base Astra. Artificial Analysis Preparedness. OpenAI rated Astra High for AI Self-Improvement, a first for one of its externally released models. On a separate measure, Vals’ RSI-Index rose from 27.07% to 29.01%, with 50% denoting its human reference. System card · Vals FrontierMath Erdős. Epoch verified seven solutions in Lean out of 68 problems. The previous best was three. Epoch What the benchmarks measure Agents’ Last Exam 1.1. OpenAI reports Astra at xhigh gained 5.2 points over GPT-6 Astra at max, using less than a third of the cost per task. It reports a 5.5-point lead over Fable 5.2 at about 5% of the cost on that test. On GDPval v2, it says Astra used 22% fewer output tokens than its predecessor. OpenAI’s results Long engineering runs. Mercor’s OpenWorldEngineer puts Astra at 67.2%, Fable 5.2 at 54.6%, and GPT-6 Astra at 44.2%. On Vals’ multi-turn Vibe Code Bench, Astra was first and Sol was third. Mercor · Vals 3D and robotics. Astra led AA-3D with 1,318, ahead of Fable at 1,271 and Sol at 1,259. On Artificial Analysis’s robotics preview, Astra scored 79 and Sol 78, ahead of Fable at 75. Artificial Analysis Research agents. On Perplexity’s WANDR, Astra scored 0.783 at about $12.54 per task. Sol reached 0.746 at about $2.65. Perplexity Early testers disagreed Matt Shumer called the models “essentially unusable” after weeks of testing and said his Opus and Fable agents rejected much of Astra’s subagent work. Review · Workflow details Pietro Schirano attributed many of his early issues to the harness. Arena’s Peter Gostev tested Astra against Fable on visual coding and singled out Astra’s SVG peacock. Schirano · Gostev The demos. Gabriel Chua built a walkable Singapore using more than 100 Codex threads. Simon Willison ran the same three.js mech prompt through several models, including Astra, Sol, Carbon and Fable. Singapore build · Same-prompt comparison Microsoft Ignite and Gemini Microsoft ships its own coding models. MAI Code 2 is for multi-step coding, and Code 2 Flash is for quicker edits. Both are available in GitHub Copilot’s model picker, Copilot Fusion and Foundry. Microsoft also announced a multimodal upgrade to its Decision model. Microsoft Copilot Fusion. Microsoft reports 71.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 with its multi-model harness, at 88% lower cost than Claude Fable 5.2 in that comparison. Jay Parikh Image editing. Artificial Analysis ranks MAI Image 2.7 first on its editing benchmark, at $34.82 per 1,000 images. Artificial Analysis Gemini Tasks. Hydrogen now powers free Tasks in six countries, including tasks that need a phone call or a text. Google also showed a new Antigravity robotics plugin with MuJoCo simulation. Sundar Pichai · Google DeepMind Agent harnesses and inference Hugging Face’s Pi adapter. A small adapter trained inside pi lifted Qwen3.8-27B from 15 to 32 solves on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks. Across that subset it made 55% fewer tool calls per task. Model card and paired results Harness costs vary sharply. Baseten measured up to a 4.4× spread in cost per passing task across its benchmark of 22 harnesses and five open models. Baseten The harness may specialize to its model. Google’s SIM keeps the rationale and outcome of prior harness edits. A harness it evolved on Opus scored 68.41 on Gemini, versus 73.89 for the starting harness. Research summary More multi-agent products. Cognition launched persistent Devin Bots. Perplexity reported that its mixed-model teams beat four instances of the lead model on Terminal-Bench and WANDR. Replit reported diminishing returns from 16 to 32 agents on NumPy tasks. Cognition · Perplexity · Replit Coordination dominated a 1,000-agent run. Hugging Face says only 40–60 agents were calling the model at any moment. They read roughly 130 tokens for every token they wrote, with merges and tests contributing to the bottleneck. Thomas Wolf A small fraction of cache misses can dominate the bill. SemiAnalysis reports that 1.8% of uncached requests accounted for roughly 15% of spend in its sample. SemiAnalysis Marin and K2 Horizon opened up their training runs. Marin released 57 intermediate Mochi checkpoints from its 535B-A23B run. The K2 report compares four model sizes trained on the same 22T tokens and describes a decoding adapter that the team says reaches 2.2× speedup. Marin · K2 Horizon Zyphra’s long-context attention. NVIDIA also has a 4B draft for Qwen3.8-27B. vLLM · Draft-model research Industry and policy NVIDIA’s first earnings after the CEO transition. Under interim CEO Colette Kress, NVIDIA posted $115.8B in quarterly revenue, up 103% year over year, and said Vera Rubin NVL72 had shipped. The board said it did not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang. NVIDIA · AP Isomorphic Labs raises $5B. Greenoaks and Sequoia co-led the Series C. The company says it will scale its drug-design platform and develop its therapeutic pipeline. Isomorphic Labs Genesis AI raises $500M. The Series A values the robotics company at $3.5B post-money. It plans to use the funding to deploy its Eno robot and expand training and data collection. items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE He @JensenHuang doesn't comprehend that he was managing other people's money in a public vehicle. There is a fiduciary responsibility, and a burden of care, that goes with that honor. The SEC is now investigating whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. --------------------- (Wall Street Journal) -- The Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, whose star chief executive Jensen Huang recently resigned after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee, according to people familiar with the matter. The civil investigation adds to the crisis facing Nvidia, whose shares have fallen more than 10% since Huang was ousted. The focus of the investigation couldn't immediately be learned but includes whether the company's disclosures misled investors, some of the people said, Just weeks ago, Nvidia was a stock-market darling at the center of the booming artificial-intelligence trade and the most valuable company in the world. But now it has faced questions from investors about its disclosures related to Huang's affairs and its sales of its chips in Asia. Nvidia had denied earlier this year that Jensen Huang had an unusual or unexpected relationship with Alice Huang, then an executive at the Singapore-based data company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials believe is working for China's intelligence services. Megaspeed was one of several companies using Nvidia chips to set up AI data centers in Southeast Asia and suspected of diverting some of the products to China. It had been under investigation by the Commerce Department since late 2024. The Justice Department is now leading multiple investigations involving Alice Huang, The Wall Street Journal has reported. Nvidia last year changed how it discloses international chip sales, eliminating a disclosure that showed its sales to Singapore, where Megaspeed was based. Since the Huang relationship was disclosed, Nvidia's business in Asia has been in the spotlight. Congress has called for investigations and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week openly questioned whether Nvidia knowingly sold powerful chips to China to lift its earnings. "What was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel." "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia," Huang said in a statement earlier Tuesday. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely."

items.title: $NVDA $TSM TSMC AND NVIDIA: THE DIVISION OF LABOR AFTER THE JENSEN TRANSITION The most critical operational learning from NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 earnings call on 11/17/26 was not a numbe
items.body: $NVDA $TSM TSMC AND NVIDIA: THE DIVISION OF LABOR AFTER THE JENSEN TRANSITION The most critical operational learning from NVIDIA's Q3 FY27 earnings call on 11/17/26 was not a number. It was a name: TSMC. THE TELL FROM THE CALL Answering Vivek Arya's question on what stays durable through the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress said: "I see right now the leadership, even from TSMC, that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us. We secured memory. We secured advanced packaging." The sentence was not in prepared remarks. It was offered, in a governance answer, as evidence that the company's moat survives the founder's exit. Of every institution Kress could have named, she named the foundry, and she named it at the level of "leadership in our offices this week," meaning the engagement is executive to executive during the transition week itself, not a standing purchase order. The same day, NVIDIA published its supply-chain release, "NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout." In it, TSMC SVP and deputy co-COO Dr. Kevin Zhang is quoted: "TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation. This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market." The release states that Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 leveraging TSMC's 5nm, 3nm, and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Zhang is the right name to notice: he is TSMC's senior executive for the technology and packaging side of the customer relationship, and his April 2026 public remarks confirmed TSMC will build advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS and 3D-IC) in Arizona before 2029, moving TSMC from pure wafer foundry toward localized one-stop service for NVIDIA and Apple. HOW A FOUNDRY CARRIES A FABLESS ROADMAP TSMC's support for NVIDIA's roadmap is not generic capacity. It operates through five concrete mechanisms. First, custom process variants built for NVIDIA alone. NVIDIA's own architecture pages state that Blackwell GPUs are "manufactured using a custom-built TSMC 4NP process," and NVIDIA's Hopper technical blog states the GH100 was "fabricated using the TSMC 4N process customized for NVIDIA." 4N was a variant of TSMC's N4 tuned for NVIDIA; 4NP refined it. A foundry does not build a named, customer-specific process flavor for a customer it treats as interchangeable. This is design-technology co-optimization in its most literal form: the process design kit, transistor tuning, and yield learning are accumulated against NVIDIA's reticle-limit dies (Blackwell is two dies, 208 billion transistors), and that accumulated learning is not transferable to another vendor on any useful timeline. Second, node sequencing locked years ahead. Vera Rubin ships on TSMC 3nm-class process (reported as N3P, a refined 3nm variant, paired with CoWoS-L packaging), with networking and other platform silicon on 5nm. Rubin Ultra follows in 2027. For Feynman (2028), multiple supply-chain reports say NVIDIA will be the first, and reportedly the only, customer for TSMC's A16 node, whose defining feature is Super Power Rail backside power delivery, worth a claimed 8 to 10% speed gain at the same voltage or 15 to 20% power reduction at the same speed against N2P per TSMC's own symposium figures. Apple is reported to skip A16 entirely and go from N2 to A14. The significance for the transition question: the Feynman decision, if the reports are right, was made inside the Huang era and binds NVIDIA to TSMC's most experimental node for 2028. Whoever the permanent CEO is, the silicon roadmap through 2028 is already a TSMC joint program. One counterweight: DigiTimes has reported NVIDIA exploring Intel EMIB packaging for a minority share (reported around 25%) of Feynman packaging, with the balance at TSMC. That reporting is single-source and unconfirmed. Even if true, it diversifies a packaging step, not the wafer or the roadmap relationship. The CPU leg of the roadmap runs through the same channel. The 11/17/26 release states that Vera CPUs, not only Rubin GPUs, began volume shipments in Q3 FY27 on TSMC process and CoWoS technologies. Management expects standalone CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028 as Vera moves from the Grace pattern (a CPU paired inside a Grace Blackwell or Vera Rubin system) toward a merchant CPU sold across cloud operators and AI customers for agent execution and orchestration workloads. That expansion is entirely fabless: every incremental Vera CPU is a TSMC wafer and, in its packaged form, CoWoS capacity. TSMC's side has publicly leaned into the same theme, with Wei's Q2 2026 call remarks on agentic CPU demand. For the transition question this matters because the CPU is the newest and least Huang-dependent leg of the roadmap: its ramp is a manufacturing and packaging execution problem of exactly the kind TSMC underwrites, rather than a founder-vision problem. Third, CoWoS allocation as the shipment governor. Advanced packaging, not wafer starts, is the binding constraint on AI accelerator shipments. TSMC's CoWoS capacity ran about 13,000 to 16,000 wafers per month in 2023, about 70,000 by end of 2025, is expected to exceed 130,000 per month by end of 2026, and to reach roughly 170,000 to 200,000 per month in 2027 depending on the estimating house (KGI at 170k, UBS at about 180k for TSMC within a 270k industry total, other supply chain estimates above 200k). Morgan Stanley's supply chain survey puts NVIDIA's share of global CoWoS demand at about 60% in 2026, easing to about 45% in 2027 as hyperscaler ASICs grow; UBS puts NVIDIA's share of CoWoS wafer demand at 65% in 2025 falling to 49% in 2027. NVIDIA is reported to have booked about 595,000 CoWoS wafers for 2026, roughly 515,000 of them from TSMC, the bulk CoWoS-L for Rubin, Vera CPUs, and GB-series parts. One arithmetic tension in the source set: 515,000 wafers against the capacity path above implies roughly 40 to 45% of TSMC's 2026 CoWoS output, below the roughly 60% demand-share survey figure. The two series most likely measure different things (surveyed demand versus booked or allocated wafers), so they should not be combined arithmetically; either way, NVIDIA is the pool's largest single claimant by a wide margin. C.C. Wei has said on an investor call that packaging capacity was "so tight that it limited customer growth." When Kress says "we secured advanced packaging," this is the asset she means: allocation inside a capacity pool that will not clear demand until 2027 at the earliest, allocated by TSMC, to the customer TSMC chooses to prioritize. Fourth, yield and ramp co-management. Vera Rubin generated nearly $20 billion of revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, the fastest ramp in NVIDIA's history. A ramp of that slope on a new platform, a new memory generation (HBM4), and CoWoS-L packaging is a joint NVIDIA-TSMC engineering exercise: defect density learning on reticle-scale dies, interposer supply (including the GlobalFoundries silicon interposer agreement inside the CoWoS ecosystem), and substrate capacity, which is why the 11/17/26 release also carries Kinsus expanding NVIDIA-dedicated substrate capacity by more than 3.5x and SPIL expanding advanced packaging under multiyear agreement with multibillion-dollar NVIDIA funding. TSMC's role in a ramp is the unglamorous one that decides whether a launch quarter is a beat or a miss: it owns the yield curve. Fifth, capacity underwriting through prepayment and commitment structures on both sides. NVIDIA's supply commitments rose from $279 billion to $390 billion in one quarter, primarily multi-year memory procurement, inside $518 billion of all-in commitments. On the capital-allocation question, Kress ranked supplier prepaids as the top operating use of capital after buybacks. TSMC's side of the same structure is its capex: the 2026 budget stands at $60 to $64 billion, with Deutsche Bank's October 2026 forecasts putting 2027 capex at $84 billion and 2028 at $100 billion (single-source analyst estimates). Wei's stated discipline is that he verifies demand personally before spending: "I want to make sure that my customers' demand are real. So I talked to those cloud service providers, all of them... they show me the evidence that the AI really helps their business." The mechanism, in one sentence: NVIDIA prepays and commits, TSMC builds and allocates, and each side's balance sheet now carries the other's forecast. WHAT TSMC HAS AT STAKE NVIDIA is now TSMC's largest customer. Analyst estimates carried by CNBC in January 2026 put NVIDIA at roughly $33 billion of TSMC revenue in 2026, about 22% of the total, against Apple's roughly $27 billion and 18%, and Huang himself confirmed the ranking on a podcast ("Morris will be happy to know NVIDIA is TSMC's largest customer now"). TSMC does not publish customer-level revenue, so the percentages are estimates, while the ranking is confirmed by Huang's own statement. One vintage warning on those figures: the January 2026 estimates imply a TSMC 2026 revenue total near $150 billion, but TSMC has since blown past that path, with Q3 2026 revenue of about $46.7 billion, Q4 guided to $52.3 to $54.3 billion, and full-year growth guidance raised to around 44%. On the current run rate, $33 billion would be a materially smaller share than 22%, so either the dollar figure is now stale and too low if the share held, or the share has eased as the rest of the HPC complex grew. The ranking is confirmed; the exact 2026 share is not. TSMC's disclosed platform mix shows the concentration underneath: HPC was 68% of revenue in Q3 2026, and NVIDIA is the largest single contributor to that platform. The Arizona program prices the stake. TSMC's US commitment stood at $165 billion (six fabs, two advanced packaging facilities, an R&D center) after the March 2025 addition of $100 billion. At the Q2 2026 earnings call, Wei announced a further $100 billion US investment, taking the Arizona total to $265 billion across 12 facilities, with dedicated CoWoS packaging capacity in Arizona aimed at the AI packaging bottleneck. Arizona's anchor demand is US AI and HPC customers; the campus exists because NVIDIA-class demand made US leading-edge capacity financeable, and its economics depend on that demand persisting at high utilization for decades. Advanced packaging is becoming a P&L line in its own right: UBS expects advanced packaging and testing to reach about 12% of TSMC's sales in 2026 and 16% in 2027. The exposure is symmetric and already visible in the tape. On 11/16/26, before NVIDIA had reported anything, Asia sold the supply chain on the NVIDIA CEO story: the Taiex fell 6.03%, its second-largest point drop on record, and TSMC fell 5.74% (exchange figures relayed across multiple accounts; treat as color, consistent across sources). TSMC's equity is, in part, a derivative of NVIDIA's stability. If NVIDIA stumbles, TSMC does not merely lose orders: it holds CoWoS capacity built for one customer's package architecture, N3 and A16 capacity sequenced around one customer's roadmap, and an Arizona gigafab cluster whose utilization case is AI demand concentrated in a handful of US customers, NVIDIA first among them. Wei's own hedge is the rest of the HPC complex (AMD, Broadcom, the hyperscaler ASIC programs all ride the same CoWoS pool, which is why NVIDIA's share falls toward 45 to 49% by 2027 even as its absolute wafers grow), plus Apple on the consumer side. But there is no second NVIDIA: no other customer accounts for roughly 60% of global CoWoS demand in the Morgan Stanley survey or anchors a custom-node program. This is the factual core underneath the claim that "they won't let $1tr of new fabs get mothballed." The trillion-dollar figure is best understood at industry scale rather than as a TSMC line item: announced US semiconductor investment

items.body: https://t.co/DrLGfxIQSU GAI DATA CENTER DEVELOPMENT DAILY DIGEST, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 2026 LEAD ITEMS - Project Jupiter, Dona Ana County, New Mexico: HSBC sold its roughly $300 million slice of the $18 billion construction financing in the mid-80s, and ING and Societe Generale are reported offering up to $800 million more of data center loans for sale, detailed under FINANCING ITEMS. NEW LAUNCHES - Giga Energy Project Clay, Hunt County, Texas, event 11/17/26, verified. Giga Energy will develop, own and operate the approximately 30 acre campus for an undisclosed US based AI cloud provider under a 10 year lease stated at $1 billion; ground was broken in July 2026 and service is expected spring 2027. Capacity is 60 MW, below the 100 MW floor, included under the strategic clause. Naming defect recorded on the finding: Giga issued two releases the same day for the same project, the morning release naming it Project Marl and the later release Project Clay; it is one campus, and the name must be resolved before any census load. The lease is also tonight's pre-leasing pass item, merged into this one finding. - Lenovo Wanquan Hybrid Token Factory Mother Plant, Zhangjiakou, Hebei, China, LATE, event 11/10/26, verified. Lenovo launched the Wanquan Hybrid Token Factory brand and signed a cooperation agreement with the Zhangjiakou municipal government for the first mother plant: an initial 15,000P heterogeneous computing cluster and an intelligent computing center of about 100 MW, phase 1 construction set for 2027. No district or parcel was published. - Meridian One, Hickstead, West Sussex, United Kingdom, LATE, event 10/26, month precision only, verified. A proposal for a phased campus at Northlands Enterprise Park with a long-term power ambition of 100 MW, five liquid-cooled buildings and a stated investment ambition above 1 billion pounds over about 10 years. The 100 MW is an ambition figure, not committed capacity, and planning permission has not yet been submitted. - NorthVault AI campus, Ontario, Canada, event 11/17/26, lead only. A newly launched firm announced an AI campus with 4 MW available now, 43.75 MW to be energized by Q3 2027, and a long-term path to 120 MW. No site location was disclosed and no operator primary document was retrieved; captured as an unverified lead. - Ixian Infrastructure, Varpaisjarvi, Lapinlahti, Finland, event 11/17/26, single-source. A planned data center across 13 hectares targeting 50 MW, with scope to reach 150 MW; the two figures are distinct and are not blended. One trade press roundup citing Yle; the Yle original was not opened. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the SpaceX linked 6 GW Cochise County, Arizona campus application (verified in October as finding 990; the Planning and Zoning Commission hearing is 12/09/26), and the AirTrunk Andhra Pradesh, Enlight Hof Shemen, and TIZA AI Gebeng items from prior runs. PROJECT EVOLUTIONS - Digital Realty Digital Park Fechenheim, Frankfurt, Germany, event 11/17/26, verified (filed under its power category in the database). The dedicated 110 kV underground connection is now operational, designed for up to 300 MVA, built over about 20 months. Campus plan: 11 data centers, up to 200 MW IT at full build-out, 3 operating, the fourth due in 2027. No Fechenheim row exists in production; the campus record is queued as a divergence for the quarterly census refresh. - Dade County Industrial Park, Georgia, event 11/17/26, single-source. The county Industrial Development Authority withdrew its letter of intent tied to the proposed Masterworks Atlanta data center (about 300 MW in prior coverage) after the countywide moratorium below. The project is on hold. - Seen tonight and already captured, not new rows: the Fermi Project Matador hyperscaler prepayment (verified finding 1655; tonight's touch records explicitly that the same 11/12/26 release terminated the TensorWave 222 MW lease and the AMD credit support, leaving Matador without a signed tenant), the Nebius Vineland slip to Q2 2027 (verified), the IREN Horizon equipment delivery delay, the AWS Hobart transformer transport delay, and the AWS Wheatfield groundbreaking of 11/12/26. BLOCKERS - No blocker was first seen tonight as its own row. The night's blocker substance is the Fermi Project Matador termination touch: the 11/12/26 Fermi release also terminated the TensorWave 222 MW lease and the AMD credit support agreement, leaving Project Matador with zero signed leases; the termination now sits on the verified prepayment finding's record, carried under PROJECT EVOLUTIONS above. REGULATORY RESTRICTIONS - Pitt County, North Carolina, LATE, event 11/16/26, verified. After the public hearing, the Board voted unanimously to adopt a two-year moratorium on data center development, tied to the county's first unified development ordinance, expected complete by the end of 2027. The Board stopped short of a ban. This resolves yesterday's watch finding. - New Braunfels, Texas, LATE, event 11/16/26, verified. City Council approved ORD26-367 on second and final reading, unanimously. The final text substitutes a 3,000-foot setback for the earlier 2,000-foot figure and adds a decommissioning plan and a surety bond requirement, on top of heavy industrial zoning with a Type 2 special use permit and a ban over the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone. This resolves the watch finding carried since 11/13/26. - Springfield, Missouri, LATE, event 11/16/26, single-source. Council voted unanimously to extend the data center administrative delay (in place since late June) to 02/24/27, and passed a substitute definition bill 6-2-1. A judge denied the developer bid to lift the moratorium on 11/09/26. - Dade County, Georgia, LATE, event 11/05/26, single-source. The county approved a 90-day moratorium countywide after the roughly 300 MW Masterworks Atlanta proposal; procedural reporting on the vote conflicts and is recorded unresolved. - United States (national), event 11/17/26, single-source. Members of Congress including Rep. McGovern rallied at the Capitol and delivered thousands of petitions demanding a national data center moratorium, backing the AI Data Center Moratorium Act. A political action, not an enacted restriction. - Loudoun County, Virginia, event 11/17/26, watch. The pause vote sat on today's agenda as item 14.m (up to 12 months per application, about 33 pending applications); the meeting ran from 4:00pm EST and no outcome was public by run time. items.body: $NVDA earnings transcript + industry read through. To sum it up: "Demand far exceeds supply". - Good news for the $MU / Samsung memory longs: "Our supply commitments increased from $279B last quarter to $390B, primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply". (from SEC filings, not call) This is a a major leap Q/Q in supply procurement. - "We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year-over-year, up from 70%." (upward revision, likely due to capacity constraints easing) (new agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional ABF substrate capacity) - NVIDIA said industry cloud backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion in a single quarter. While GPU rental pricing is continuing to rise dramatically: Hopper GPUs: 2x their original pricing B300 GPUs: +60% since introduction Utilization: NVIDIA says its own compute is fully utilized across the hyperscalers and neoclouds it serves. - "Our co-packaged optics roadmap remains on track" Optical networking keeps growing rapidly ($21B+ in quarterly networking), CPO scale out switches has entered volume production. With Lambda earlier announcing production deployment of Nvidia photonics CPO switches. - "Under these agreements, we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure" So there's additional recurring economics coming from Neoclouds. But just points to industry acceleration from memory to CPO to neoclouds, relative to markets pricing in collapse.

items.body: 🔔 The Daily Semi-Cap — November 17, 2026 📊 SMH: $460.10 (-0.39% vs prior trading close) • Nvidia’s fiscal Q3 revenue reached $115.8B, up 103% YoY, with Data Center at $107.6B and adjusted EPS of $2.68. Q4 guidance is $130B ±3%, including an extra week and no China Data Center compute revenue. Gross margin is guided to 71–72%, versus 74.9% adjusted this quarter. • Vertiv expanded its 800 VDC portfolio from racks into compute pods and data halls. A new 5MW solid-state transformer targets up to 98% conversion efficiency while removing two to three conversion stages. Pilots and validation are underway; the opportunity is a simpler, denser AI power train. • Nvidia is backing new substrate and packaging capacity. Kinsus plans more than 3.5x its Nvidia-dedicated ABF capacity, with production beginning H2 2027 and added capacity targeted for Q3 2028. SPIL’s new multibillion-dollar agreement expands dedicated advanced packaging by mid-2029, extending investment visibility across the supply chain. • Arista launched Etherlink R4 routing platforms for distributed inference, using 5nm silicon and a 25.6Tbps optical line system. Arista claims up to 60% lower power than older-node alternatives. Most products are available now; 7020HR4 follows in early 2027. The target is secure, low-latency inference across geographically separated clusters. • Giga Energy signed a 10-year, $1B lease with an undisclosed U.S. AI cloud provider for its 60MW Project Clay campus in Texas. Service is targeted for spring 2027. Factory-built infrastructure and closed-loop cooling aim to shorten construction while avoiding local water consumption for compute cooling. • PJM’s newly detailed grid proposals target a one-year combined study process for large loads and generation, roughly halving current timelines. Separately proposed ride-through requirements would keep large computing facilities connected during disturbances. Both await regulatory action; faster studies alone will not deliver generation or eliminate upgrade costs. • Trinity Capital committed $100M in debt financing to Phononic for manufacturing expansion. Its solid-state thermal controls target GPUs, HBM, networking silicon and optical transceivers. More capital is flowing toward component-level cooling as thermal constraints increasingly affect usable compute capacity and optical performance.

items.title: THERMAL ALERT: KERCH STRAIT BRIDGE, RUSSIA SITE • Kerch Strait Bridge (Crimean Bridge), Russia and occupied Crimea, 19 km road-and-rail crossing of the Kerch Strait; the navigation
items.body: THERMAL ALERT: KERCH STRAIT BRIDGE, RUSSIA SITE • Kerch Strait Bridge (Crimean Bridge), Russia and occupied Crimea, 19 km road-and-rail crossing of the Kerch Strait; the navigational arch span crosses the Kerch-Yenikale Canal, the main deepwater passage between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea • Russia's only road and rail link to Crimea and its main military logistics artery to the peninsula • The bridge is not a refining or energy site: this analysis runs on a post by sentdefender (11/17/26 3:42 PM EDT) claiming a missile strike collapsed the arch and roadway DETECTION • FIRMS thermal pull over the bridge corridor (lat 45.24 to 45.37, lon 36.44 to 36.62), 11/15/26 to 11/17/26, VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS: zero detections • A structural collapse with brief impact fires is a weak thermal target, so the null carries little weight either way; the event is established by wire reporting and verified imagery, not by thermal satellite • Sentinel-2 imagery from 10/26/26 shows the arch span intact over the canal, protective booms in the water; the first clear post-event pass is still pending CONFIDENCE • Event real at the site: HIGH, 95%+ • Cause (Ukrainian drone and missile strike): HIGH, 90-95% • Damage (road arch and span collapsed, road link severed; rail arch damaged, rail bridge standing): HIGH, 85-90% • The sentdefender video as evidence of the strike: LOW, under 10% • Rationale: claimant and target state agree on the event, and Reuters verified the imagery Kyiv published. The residual uncertainty is in the details (weapon mix, repair time), not the event. His video, by contrast, is an Exilenova+ watermarked montage set to an Eminem track; frame by frame it shows distant night explosions and one fire filmed through industrial pipe racks, a plant, not a bridge. No bridge, arch, or collapse appears in it. CORROBORATION • X: the primary material is Zelenskyy's own posts with video, verified by Reuters; Ukraine's General Staff stated on X that the arch and span collapsed and no vehicle can cross; sentdefender relayed the claim this afternoon, after the wires; Russian monitoring channels, via NOELreports, warn of a possible further FP-5 attack tonight • Officials: Russia's Transport Ministry confirmed damage and suspended traffic, with rail resumed on one track today (Interfax); the Investigative Committee called it a terrorist act; Aksyonov confirmed the attack and reported two killed elsewhere in Crimea; Peskov promised a repair plan • Web: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg News and the FT all carry the collapse, the SBU's seven-stage operation account (Palianytsia drones on the road section, Neptune and Ruta and FP-5 on the rail section, Flamingo the final blow; seven of nine missiles that hit were Ruta), and Ambrey's note that the fallen arch blocks the Kerch-Yenikale Canal; Russia's MoD claimed 1,441 drones intercepted overnight, the largest barrage of the war, and this was the second strike on the bridge in two nights • Status: VERIFIED; road section destroyed at the arch span, rail damaged but operating on one track. Kyiv's year-plus repair estimate for the fallen roughly 6,000-tonne structure is a claimant figure, unverified WHY IT MATTERS • Crimea logistics: with the road link severed and rail on one track, fuel and military supply into Crimea shifts to ferries and the land corridor; Crimea fuel tightness, with retail restrictions already across six-plus Russian regions, gets worse. That supports the product-tightness side of the refining picture even as the paper crack sells off • Azov transit: debris in the canal impairs Azov port flows (Rostov, Azov, Taganrog) days after a FIRMS-verified fire at the Azov oil depot; the campaign is now working the whole Azov-Crimea logistics chain, and a third attempt tonight is openly warned of on Russian channels • Timing: two days before the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen, a spectacular escalation that cuts against the peace-process repricing pressuring cracks this week Coordinates: 45.3086, 36.5064

items.title: Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI. For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension:
items.body: Agent swarms are the next scaling frontier for AI. For years, we’ve scaled intelligence by training larger models and giving them more time to think. But there’s another dimension: running many agents in parallel, exploring different approaches, challenging each other, and working together on solutions that no single agent could easily discover. OpenAI has already demonstrated the potential of this approach with breakthroughs in mathematics. Until now, experimenting with agent swarms yourself required building complicated orchestration infrastructure. Starting today on Replit, spinning up a swarm of agents is just one prompt away. Excited to see what people discover when we make collective machine intelligence programmable by anyone.

SaaS gave us a lot of trade-able volatility in 2026, but I generally lean short from here.

items.title: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE MUDDY WATERS IS SHORT NVIDIA: THE PURI QUESTION, EXPLAINED WHAT WAS PUBLISHED • At 2:53 PM ET today, November 17, 2026, hours before Nvidia reports third quar
items.body: $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE MUDDY WATERS IS SHORT NVIDIA: THE PURI QUESTION, EXPLAINED WHAT WAS PUBLISHED • At 2:53 PM ET today, November 17, 2026, hours before Nvidia reports third quarter earnings, Muddy Waters Research disclosed that it is short Nvidia. • The disclosure is a single post: a photograph of a man and a woman at a formal event, the firm's standard short disclosure, and a question it pointedly does not answer. • The man is Ajay K. Puri, until this summer the likely third most senior executive at Nvidia, per Muddy Waters. The open question is the identity of the woman with him. THE NVIDIA EXECUTIVE • Ajay "Jay" Puri joined Nvidia in 2005 and ran worldwide field operations, the organization that sells Nvidia's chips and systems and manages its customer relationships, for 21 years. • Per Muddy Waters, Puri ranked behind only Jensen Huang and Colette Kress. His total compensation ran slightly above Kress's in fiscal 2024 through 2026, and he was one of only five executives named in the company's 2026 proxy. • On June 28, 2026, Puri told Nvidia he would retire from the operating role. The company disclosed it in a filing dated July 2. He remains a senior advisor. Nicholas Parker, hired from Microsoft, took over field operations in late August. • Puri was already in this week's news. The New York Post reported on November 14 that in a closed-door meeting in February, in front of more than 30 executives, Huang allegedly told Puri, "I hope you die and put us all out of our misery." Nothing in Nvidia's filing connects the retirement to that meeting. THE PHOTOGRAPHS • Muddy Waters says a woman identified as Cenly Chen, and referred to in some photograph tags as Cenly Puri, has been photographed in public with Puri between 2024 and 2026. • The firm then asks, in its own words, whether the woman in the photographs is the same Cenly Chen who used to work at Super Micro Computer. • That question is the entire assertion. Everything else is the public record of the other Cenly Chen. THE SUPER MICRO EXECUTIVE • Cenly Chen was Super Micro's Senior Vice President and Chief Growth Officer. She reported directly to CEO Charles Liang and led Sales Team #1, which generated approximately 80% of the company's total sales. • The consolidated class action complaint against Super Micro, filed October 9, 2026 in the Northern District of California (Case No. 3:26-cv-02606-JSC), builds its account of Chen on confidential former employees. Their allegations are unproven and untested in court: • FE-1, a former sales director: Chen "had a very close relationship with NVIDIA and managed the Company's acquisition of GPU chips from NVIDIA." Because supply was limited, "NVIDIA would allocate a certain number to Super Micro, and Chen decided how to distribute them among Super Micro's customers." • FE-4: "the Company's relationship with NVIDIA was managed by Cenly Chen, who handled all allocations of NVIDIA chips to Super Micro," and "there was no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge of the Company's illicit sales." • Two witnesses describe the same incident: Chen carried Nvidia chips to San Francisco and handed them to a CoreWeave executive as he was boarding a plane to China, so CoreWeave could test them at its facilities. • FE-1 further states that Chen left in May 2026, after the diversion scheme became public, and that it was widely known inside the company that she had to go because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips bearing serial numbers associated with GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China, and that she resigned so the company could claim no current employees were involved in the scheme for which Liaw was arrested. FE-4 states her departure was directly related to the government's investigation. • A shareholder derivative complaint filed on October 15, 2026 repeats the account, including the allegation that Chen was forced to resign after the indictment. THE INDICTMENT UNDERNEATH IT • On March 19, 2026, the Justice Department unsealed an indictment of three people associated with Super Micro: co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw, Taiwan office general manager Ruei-Tsang "Steven" Chang, and third-party broker Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun. • The charge: conspiring to divert Super Micro servers containing Nvidia GPUs to customers in China without a Commerce Department license, approximately $2.5 billion of servers across 2024 and 2025. Per the complaint, one channel ran through a Thai pass-through company, Obon, that repackaged servers in unmarked boxes to obscure their contents and destination. By Super Micro's fiscal fourth quarter of 2024, Obon was its eleventh most profitable customer worldwide, at roughly $99.7 million of reported revenue in that quarter alone. • Super Micro itself was not charged. Its stock fell 33.3%, to $20.53, on the news. WHY THE QUESTION MATTERS • GPU allocation was the scarcest resource in the AI buildout, and it ran through two desks. On the Nvidia side, allocations to customers sat inside the field operations organization Puri ran for two decades. On the Super Micro side, per the complaint, every allocation decision sat with Chen. • If the woman in the photographs is Chen, the people on opposite sides of that table were photographed together as a couple throughout 2024 to 2026, the exact window of the alleged diversion, and both left their jobs within weeks of each other after the indictment: Chen in May 2026, Puri in June 2026. • If she is not Chen, Muddy Waters has published a photograph of a private citizen next to a short disclosure, and the story collapses to nothing. The firm knows this. It published anyway, and it disclosed its position in the same post. THE WEEK IT LANDED IN • Monday: the Commerce and Justice Departments said in a joint statement that a federal investigation into the diversion of Nvidia chips, opened in 2024, is now a Justice Department led criminal investigation, and that BIS officers conducted an on-site end-use check in Singapore in June 2025 as part of it. • Monday: BIS issued its remote access rule, closing the offshore rental channel for advanced chips destined for data centers serving Chinese parents. • This morning: Nvidia's board created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. • Tonight: Colette Kress, interim CEO since Huang's resignation last week, delivers her first earnings report, and the channel question is the one she is most likely to be pressed on. • A year ago, Muddy Waters founder Carson Block said that anyone out there shorting Nvidia or the other big tech leaders "is not going to be in business very long." Today his firm is short the largest of them, into a binary print, on a channel integrity thesis rather than a valuation one. WHAT THIS IS NOT • Muddy Waters does not claim to have proven the identity. It asks the question. • No government has accused Cenly Chen of any crime. She is not indicted. Neither is Puri, and the post alleges no act by him beyond being photographed. • The complaint's passages about Chen are plaintiff allegations sourced to confidential witnesses. They have not been tested in court. • There is no revenue figure in this story, no allegation that Nvidia as a company directed any diversion, and no new government action against Nvidia. Tonight's print still turns on the numbers and the guidance. WHAT TO WATCH • Any statement from Nvidia, Puri, or Chen confirming or denying the identity. A denial ends it. Silence extends it. • The shape of an Nvidia denial is already on the record in the Taiwan prosecution arising from the same diversion channels: the company said it had investigated thoroughly and found no indication its employee knew of the alleged diversion effort by employees at other companies. • Whether Kress addresses channel controls and end-use verification on tonight's call, and what the 10-Q's legal proceedings section adds. • Whether the board's new oversight committee takes up the sales organization, and not only the former CEO.
