external_articles.title: Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development
external_articles.body:
Small LoRA adapters, trained with reinforcement learning inside pi, opencode and hermes, all served from one model, with every tool call the model makes inspected by safeagents before it runs. Follow the training runs on the live dashboard .

The same model behaves differently in different agent harnesses, where each one has its own tools, prompt and control flow. The ultimate guide to multi-harness RL showed how to train a model inside the harnesses themselves, without modifying them.

Here, we take a different approach, we train a small LoRA adapter per harness, on top of a base model. People can then swap the model behind their local agent for the adapter trained in that agent.

We first released initial harness adapters for LFM2.5-24B-A2B only, trained under pi, hermes and claude-code. They gave positive signals, both in tool-calling efficiency and in accuracy on held-out tasks, and given their adoption by the community, we decided to push further in this direction and add new components to the RL training, to make our initial work more complete.

LoRA adapters are cost-efficient for training and evaluation, since one server can host every harness's policy at once. At inference, anyone can load the adapter for the harness of their choice, to make the base model more efficient on their use case. We detail in One base model, many adapters how exactly we leverage LoRA adapters for training and evaluation.

We increased the diversity and difficulty of our previous RL tasks by generating synthetic RL environments, with open-source agent trajectories (a trajectory being the full logs of an agent session: the user requests, the model replies and every tool call with its output) as seed data. We derived four types of RL environments:

This animated demo shows what each type of task looks like:

How these environments are built, checked and scored is in Environments .

RL also lets the model hack the reward, taking shortcuts on the task it's trying to solve. So we plug safeagents into the RL training stage. It inspects the model's tool calls and blocks the ones that are clearly attempts at reward hacking. A blocked call is replaced by a text explaining why it was blocked, which invites the model to explore a different path. How the checks work, and a call they blocked, is in Saying 🙅 to agent shortcuts .

After feedback from the community, we extended the set of models we train to LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM3-1.7B , plus TwIL-8B as an experiment. The model card states it was not trained on agentic data, and we want to know whether such a model gives positive signals and can produce harness adapters too. The models and their settings are in Trained models .

We train our models with the GRPO algorithm, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer together with tree attention for efficient training. Our harness adapters are LoRA adapters with rank 32, attached on every linear layer ( all-linear ). The models perform 8 rollouts per task, and we use a learning rate of 1e-5 for all our trainings.

Each run mixes SmolDataEnvs tasks, weighted toward medium and hard ones, with 230 of the 270 Repo2RLEnvs tasks. The other 40 Repo2RLEnvs tasks, and 150 SmolDataEnvs tasks, are held out for evaluation and never trained on.

Some shared parameters are the following: sampling temperature 0.8, up to 32,768 output tokens per turn, rollouts at most 4 weight updates stale, 4 gradient-accumulation steps, and a checkpoint every 10 steps, each one evaluated. TwIL gets 30 agent steps per session and 20 minutes timeout as it needs more steps to tasks (since not trained on agentic data).

We train on HF Jobs : 2×H200 for LFM3-1.7B, and 4×H200 for the other runs. The total cost of each training run is shown on the live dashboard of the training jobs.

Adapters pay off in two places, both shown below: switch between the training and evaluation modes. The sections below break each one down.

Each model is served by one vLLM. Its three trainers, one per harness, all send rollouts to it, each request naming its own adapter, so the base weights are loaded once for all three. After a gradient step, the trainer loads its new adapter into vLLM by name, next to the current one. Requests already running on the old version finish on it, so nothing pauses.

For LFM3-1.7B, the three trainers even share one GPU: an agent rollout spends most of its time in the sandbox, not generating, so the trainers mostly wait. In earlier runs a trainer spent about 35 s per step in forward and backward passes, against several minutes waiting for rollouts. Three of them take turns instead of idling on their own.

Training is asynchronous, where the rollouts and gradient steps don't wait for each other. Each trainer keeps up to 48 agent sessions running at once, about 6 tasks with 8 rollouts each (12 sessions for TwIL-8B, whose long reasoning fills vLLM's memory sooner). A task joins the training queue once all 8 of its rollouts are scored, since GRPO compares them with each other.

A gradient step packs finished rollouts into 4 micro-batches, each up to a token budget: 131,072 tokens for LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 65,536 for LFM3-1.7B and TwIL-8B. So the number of tasks per step isn't fixed: short sessions fit many, long ones few. Our earlier LFM2.5-24B-A2B runs trained on about 8 tasks (64 rollouts) per step, TwIL-8B's smoke run on about one. After the step, the new adapter version is loaded into vLLM, and rollouts started more than 4 versions earlier are dropped, so the model never learns from a policy too far behind it.

The dashboard logs both numbers for every run: batch/groups_per_step (tasks) and batch/samples_per_step (rollouts). They also set how often a task comes back: at 8 tasks per step, LFM2.5-24B-A2B's 200 steps go over its 530 tasks about 3 times.

The same trick evaluates every checkpoint at once. One vLLM loads the base weights, then each checkpoint as an adapter, with one sandbox server per checkpoint running its held-out tasks in parallel. Nine checkpoints of LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 1,350 agent sessions in all, ran in a single H200 job in under an hour, for about $5 of GPU time. Merging each checkpoint into full weights and serving them one by one would have cost about $90. And a score measures the adapter exactly as it was trained (nothing is merged or converted).

The raw material is agent sessions that people published on the Hugging Face Hub, from pi, Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses. They are converted to ATIF trajectories, then each one goes through the same six steps. A candidate that fails any of them is dropped, with its reason recorded.

Let's now dive into how the task type ( repair , qa , build , extend ) is decided. No LLM is involved in this stage: the replayed trajectory already records every command the agent ran, its exit code and the files before it, plus where each user request starts. Each type is a simple rule over those facts, so the same trajectory always yields the same candidates:

The LLM only comes in afterwards, where understanding is needed: writing the contract and tests for a candidate that's already typed.

Every task ships an oracle: a reference solution, in solution/ , that must score full reward in the task's own image, or the task is dropped. In almost every case, the oracle is not written by the LLM: it's the original agent's own work, taken from the trajectory, where it really happened and passed its checks.

So the teacher LLM writes the exam, and the trajectory provides the answer key it's checked against. For build and extend , a test is kept only if it passes on the oracle twice and fails on a stub (the same interface with no behaviour) and on an empty workspace, and the kept tests must catch most deliberately injected bugs. A wrong test fails on the oracle and is dropped; a test too weak to tell real code from a stub is dropped too.

Pick a task and a file to read it as the agent and the verifier see it. These five come from harness-hub/traj2envs-rl , one per task type and difficulty level in the release.

The release is far from balanced: 253 of its 270 tasks are build tasks (94%), against 11 repair , 6 extend and no qa . We still describe qa to share the full environment generation recipe, and we plan to include more of these tasks in future releases. 243 of the 270 come from one source, TeichAI/Ox-Alpha-Pi-Traces, and 238 of those are build . The skew comes from what shared trajectories contain, and from how strict each task type is:

The difficulty labels lean the same way: 179 tasks are easy for LFM2.5-24B-A2B, 61 medium and 30 hard. That's why each run's mix weights SmolDataEnvs toward medium and hard tasks, and why we'd like more repair and extend tasks: they need sessions where something goes wrong and gets fixed, or where a project grows over several requests. Sharing such sessions, scrubbed with safeagents, is the most useful contribution.

Each task records how often a reference agent solves it, and the training mix favours tasks that are solved sometimes but not always: GRPO only learns from groups where some rollouts pass and others fail. Repo2RLEnvs is moving to Repo2RLEnv , and its repository will be archived.

RL finds shortcuts: a policy rewarded for passing tests will, sooner or later, try to read the tests, rewrite them, or fetch the answer from wherever the task came from. So every tool call goes through safeagents before the harness runs it.

safeagents is a reverse proxy: a small server placed in front of another one, that clients talk to as if it were the real thing. The harness's base URL points at safeagents instead of vLLM. Each request goes through unchanged; each response comes back through it, and the tool calls in it are checked before the harness sees them. Neither the harness nor vLLM knows it's there, and it speaks both the OpenAI Chat Completions and the Anthropic Messages APIs, streaming or not. In training, it runs on a background thread of the trainer.

Every check is a rule, not a model: the same call always gets the same verdict, in about 10 to 20 ms, and the policy can't talk its way past it. Each tool call goes through three stages, in order:

A blocked call is replaced, in the response, by a text notice: [safeagents] blocked call to `bash`: … , and a "tool use" stop becomes a plain stop. Nothing runs. The reward function gives 0 to any rollout that contains a notice, and since the token ids and logprobs pass through untouched, the trainer still trains on the blocked tokens: GRPO pushes the attempt down.

We didn't have to wait long to see it work. In TwIL-8B's smoke run, at step 0, before any update, the model was working on a SmolDataEnvs task: answer a question about a Kaggle dataset. Instead of computing the answer, it went looking for the Hugging Face bucket the task's data was staged from, where the original notebook might be:

The command names jupyter-agent-kaggle , one of the sources our SmolDataEnvs plugin lists. The call never ran, pi received the notice, and the rollout scored 0. A model that searches for answers at step 0 is the reason the guard is on from the first step, not added once something goes wrong.

atif-scan's built-in rules know about benchmarks in general, not about where our tasks' answers live. A plugin adds that: a Python module whose factory returns extra detectors, loaded with --plugin MODULE:FACTORY . Ours are three regexes each, matched only against what the agent writes (commands, tool arguments, file contents, search queries and URLs), never against what tools return:

Since every run mixes both environments, the trainer loads both plugins:

Loading them together needed one fix. SmolDataEnvs ' rule first matched any grader.py , and a Repo2RLEnvs build task asks the agent to write exactly that: a small auto-grading library. The rule would have scored correct work 0. It now matches only /tests/grader , where the SmolDataEnvs grader lives. Rescanned with both plugins, 213 agent sessions on Repo2RLEnvs tasks match none of their rul

items.body: Astera Labs $ALAB CEO Jitendra Mohan at TomorrowX Summit. The reason he started the company nine years ago was fascinating. He anticipated that the world would need far more GPUs, and connecting them would become a major challenge. Astera started with retimers. As GPU clusters grow and data rates increase, copper eventually runs into physical limitations. Optics becomes necessary. Astera is already expanding into silicon photonics, VCSEL-based connectivity, NPO, and CPO. I don't think $ALAB should be viewed as just a retimer company anymore. The AI infrastructure race is increasingly about how efficiently GPUs communicate with each other. More GPUs. More connectivity. More opportunity.

items.title: Next at TomorrowX Summit: Dina Powell McCormick, President & Vice Chairman of Meta $META. The conversation began with AI infrastructure. Data center development has become a politi
items.body: Next at TomorrowX Summit: Dina Powell McCormick, President & Vice Chairman of Meta $META. The conversation began with AI infrastructure. Data center development has become a political issue in the US, including during the recent midterm elections. Communities are concerned about electricity costs, jobs, and whether they will actually benefit from these massive investments. Dina highlighted Meta's investment in Richland Parish, Louisiana. Increased local tax revenues have helped fund substantial teacher bonuses, creating tangible benefits for the community. She also emphasized the importance of working with Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry. Data centers aren't just buildings filled with GPUs. They require electricians, fiber technicians, construction workers, and many other skilled professionals. AI infrastructure can create American jobs. But her bigger point was national security. If America cannot maintain its own computing infrastructure, its economic competitiveness and security could be at risk. Sovereign compute matters. She also expressed confidence in Meta's approach to AI safety and emphasized the importance of security. But the most powerful moment for me was a video about Meta AI glasses. A military veteran who lost his eyesight in a bunker explosion was shown using AI glasses to read letters, navigate restaurant menus with his wife, and find clothing. This is what meaningful AI looks like. Dina also spoke about raising six daughters in a world changing incredibly fast. Young people need to become AI-literate, but human skills, particularly emotional intelligence, may become even more valuable. As AI makes technical capabilities more accessible, uniquely human qualities could matter more. After listening to several CEOs today, I'm noticing a common theme. When discussing the future of AI, the conversation eventually returns to biology, medicine, science, jobs, and human lives. The real value of AI won't be measured solely by how many GPUs we deploy. It will be measured by what we accomplish with that compute.

items.title: OPTICAL NETWORKING DAILY DIGEST, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 2026 NEW PRODUCT • Arista Networks: Arista Networks announced an expanded Etherlink R4 portfolio for distributed AI inferenci
items.body: OPTICAL NETWORKING DAILY DIGEST, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 2026 NEW PRODUCT • Arista Networks: Arista Networks announced an expanded Etherlink R4 portfolio for distributed AI inferencing on November 17, 2026. Three new products: (1) 7282R4, a routing platform with dual Supervisor Engines for redundant control planes, available now; (2) the Etherlink pluggable optical line system, a 25.6 Tbps optical amplifier supporting the full C-band with muxes and demuxes for ZR/ZR+ coherent aggregation, plus a pluggable OTDR for in-service optical test, available now; (3) 7020HR4, a compact routing platform with integrated MACsec and IPsec, available in early 2027. The R4 platforms are built on 5nm silicon with up to 60 percent lower power than 7nm or 16nm alternatives. external_articles.title: 800Gbps Optical Network Interface Card for AI Data Centers by 1Finity
external_articles.body:
800Gbps Optical Network Interface Card – 1Finity, a Fujitsu company and leading global network solutions provider, today announced the development of the 1Finity Ultra Optical System™ N100 (1Finity NIC), an optical network interface card (1) that enables direct, high-speed, and low-latency optical connections between data centers. 1Finity will begin accepting advance orders in November 2026 and will gradually roll out the product ahead of its global availability starting in April 2027 (2) .

The 1Finity NIC is the world’s first optical network interface card capable of achieving high-speed connectivity of up to 800Gbps over distances of approximately 100km (3) .

The rapid proliferation of AI technology has led to a surge in demand for computational resources and data processing. Data centers currently face constraints regarding power consumption and physical space, fueling the need to distribute computational resources across multiple locations. Strategies like Watt-Bit synergy (4) —which links renewable-energy-rich regions with high-demand urban areas via high-speed networks—are gaining traction.

However, conventional Ethernet communication often suffers from performance degradation due to latency and packet loss over long distances. This leads to increased idle time for GPUs in large-scale AI processing, preventing full utilization of resources. 1Finity developed the 1Finity NIC to resolve these challenges by leveraging technologies from the NEDO Green Innovation Fund project, “Development of Next-Generation Green Data Center Technologies.”

The 1Finity NIC is a network interface card equipped with 1Finity’s proprietary xRDMA (Extend Remote Direct Memory Access) data transfer technology, which enables high-speed, low-latency transfer of large volumes of data over long distances, as well as a high-speed optical interface.

The 1Finity NIC is compliant with PCI Express, a widely adopted server expansion interface, and can be easily installed in compatible existing servers. For example, even between geographically separated data centers, users can easily connect remote servers simply by installing the 1Finity NIC in servers at each location, without the need for adjustments based on transmission distance or changes in network traffic.  This facilitates the efficient utilization of geographically distributed computing resources and data in computing environments that require large-volume data transfers, including AI training and inference.

The key features of the 1Finity NIC are as follows:

1. 400Gbps × 2-port high-speed optical interface Equipped with two 400Gbps QSFP56-DD (5) interfaces, the card supports network connectivity of up to 800Gbps in total. This enables high-speed transfer of large volumes of data generated between GPU servers during AI training and inference, helping to minimize reductions in GPU utilization caused by communication wait times. It also enables computing resources distributed across multiple data centers to work together, allowing them to be efficiently utilized for large-scale AI processing.

2. xRDMA enables high-throughput data transfer over long distances 1Finity’s proprietary xRDMA data transfer technology mitigates the impact of communication latency and packet loss associated with longer transmission distances, maintaining high data transfer efficiency even between geographically separated data centers. This enables efficient transfer of large volumes of data between computing resources such as GPUs and CPUs, even between data centers located approximately 100 km apart, supporting AI training and inference as well as distributed database processing.

1Finity will continue to expand the use cases of the 1Finity NIC through collaborative verification with customers. By seamlessly connecting data centers, 1Finity aims to realize next-generation AI infrastructure that leverages distributed computational resources with high efficiency.

For more information visit: https://www.1finity.com/ .

external_articles.title: Ekinops unveils PTM300 compact modular platform for ultra-high-capacity datacenter connectivity
external_articles.body:
New 3RU* optical platform delivers up to 32 Tb/s capacity with ultra-low power consumption per bit, open management and multi-vendor interoperability

PARIS , Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ekinops (Euronext Paris - FR0011466069 – EKI), a leading provider of optical networks, connectivity and SASE cybersecurity solutions for telecom service providers and enterprises, today announces the release of PTM300 , a new compact modular optical platform designed for high-capacity datacenter interconnect (DCI) and scale-across optical networking applications.

Designed to bring carrier-class optical transport into a datacenter form factor, PTM300 delivers up to 32 Tb/s of client and line capacity in just 3RU, supporting up to 40 x 800 Gb/s coherent pluggable interfaces.

The platform combines ultra-high density and ultra-low 0.08W per Gbps (watts per gigabit per second) power consumption with redundant power and cooling, front-to-back airflow, and Open management interface based on Openconfig and Netconf/Yang for easy integration into open, standards-based environments. It is also compatible with Ekinops' Celestis NMS for unified network management within an Ekinops optical network further simplifying integration.

With PTM300, Ekinops is extending its optical networking portfolio to address increasing interconnection bandwidth requirements between datacenters with compact modular platforms that seamlessly enable the transition from the telco environment.

High density without compromising openness and performance

PTM300 can be deployed over direct fiber, existing Ekinops optical line systems or third-party infrastructure using alien wavelengths. Beyond DCI, it is designed to address metro, regional and long-haul transport applications as well as service regeneration for router-hosted IPoWDM applications.

"The rapid growth of cloud and AI is creating unprecedented bandwidth requirements between data centers, as well a greater demand for service providers to deliver wavelength services to these locations. With PTM300, we are bringing together ultra-high capacity, ultra-low power consumption, operational simplicity and openness in a compact platform designed to help operators scale their optical networks while protecting existing infrastructure investments," said Philippe Moulin, Chief Operating Officer of Ekinops.

PTM300 will be generally available in December 2026 with first customer deployments expected in Q1 2027.

All press releases are published after Euronext Paris market close.

items.title: Michael Dell, founder and CEO of Dell Technologies $DELL, at TomorrowX Summit. Gavin Baker of Atreides Management opened with an interesting question. Over the past five years, Del
items.body: Michael Dell, founder and CEO of Dell Technologies $DELL, at TomorrowX Summit. Gavin Baker of Atreides Management opened with an interesting question. Over the past five years, Dell has outperformed every Magnificent Seven stock except NVIDIA. Why haven't other server competitors achieved similar results? Michael Dell pointed to the company's longstanding foundation in servers, storage, and data center infrastructure. Long before the AI boom, Dell had already established deep relationships with national laboratories and enterprise customers. That foundation is now a major advantage in the AI infrastructure race. Then Gavin asked an even more interesting question. "What if we're at peak AI right now?" Michael Dell strongly disagreed. For that to happen, the fundamental thesis behind AI would have to be wrong. His reasoning was fascinating. Humans are naturally curious. We constantly want to discover more and solve problems we haven't yet figured out. Biology, materials science, and scientific research still have countless unanswered questions. And AI could drive much of the progress in these fields. He expects AI to become increasingly efficient while delivering substantial benefits to the US economy. What I find particularly interesting is that Dell doesn't build frontier AI models. Regardless of who wins the AI model race, computing infrastructure remains essential. While Wall Street continues debating peak AI capex, the founder of one of the world's largest server suppliers seems convinced that AI is still in its early stages. Perhaps the more important question isn't when AI infrastructure investment peaks, but how much scientific progress AI has yet to unlock.

items.body: devin bots are multi-agent teams done right: - always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI) - own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others) - manages teams of subagents (and reviews itself) - available everywhere (call text slack whatever hello @interaction) - consistent reporting thru interactive artifacts aka devinapps not long chats (HTML is all you need™ @trq212) this is the preview that @walden_yan gave at AIE. i've been trialing them for a week and i've been able to hand over my AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation, and video editing work (also simultaneously moving from local agent worktree hell to cloud because ofc this is all cloud based thank god) hyped concepts this replaces: - /goal - "ultracode" / "ultra mode" - "loop engineering" - "agent to agent" - "agent swarms" - AI employees (see below) my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol. if youre a startup, reminder that Devin for Startups offers 65k in credits. apply via clanker

items.body: Conditions for agentic commerce "So the opportunities for third-party agentic commerce to gain traction mostly exist where these trade-offs either converge in consumer welfare or are imperceptible. items.title: AMD $AMD CEO Lisa Su at TomorrowX Summit. A few interesting takeaways. First, she was asked about Jensen Huang. Rather than directly commenting on Jensen, she shifted the conversat
items.body: AMD $AMD CEO Lisa Su at TomorrowX Summit. A few interesting takeaways. First, she was asked about Jensen Huang. Rather than directly commenting on Jensen, she shifted the conversation toward the importance of AI and the industry's future. She also emphasized the need to navigate geopolitical challenges carefully. Now, the technology. 1. CPUs still matter. While CPU market growth has been in the single digits, Lisa suggested that momentum has been strengthening recently. Even in the GPU-driven AI era, CPUs remain essential. 2. Democratizing AI. Lisa emphasized her passion for solving problems from an engineer's and scientist's perspective. For AMD, democratizing AI means making powerful computing resources accessible to more researchers and developers. She highlighted supercomputing, national laboratories, healthcare, and scientific research. The bigger vision is AI that can improve real lives, including those of our families. 3. Why Xilinx and FPGAs matter. Lisa highlighted the strategic importance of AMD's Xilinx acquisition. In her words, 1 + 1 is better than 3. Building AMD's full technology roadmap requires more than CPUs and GPUs. Modern data centers need CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and heterogeneous computing architectures working together. AMD isn't simply trying to compete with NVIDIA GPU against GPU. It's building a broader computing platform spanning CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and supercomputing. A different approach to the future of AI infrastructure.

items.body: Goldman Sachs $GS CEO David Solomon at TomorrowX Summit. Interestingly, he shared a perspective on Jensen Huang similar to what I heard earlier from Altimeter CEO Brad Gerstner. Wall Street appears to be taking the question of NVIDIA's future without Jensen seriously. Then Gavin Baker of Atreides Management asked where AI could have its greatest impact. Solomon pointed to biology and cancer research. That caught my attention. So far, AI investment has largely revolved around GPUs, data centers, power, and networking. But the next question is what AI can actually deliver in the real world. If AI can meaningfully accelerate drug discovery and cancer research, the implications could be enormous. Interesting to hear the CEO of Goldman Sachs highlight biology and cancer when discussing AI's future.

items.title: Interesting insights from Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, at TomorrowX Summit. Gerstner is an Anthropic investor and has also been closely involved in the Trump Accounts i
items.body: Interesting insights from Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, at TomorrowX Summit. Gerstner is an Anthropic investor and has also been closely involved in the Trump Accounts initiative. First, Anthropic's compute allocation caught my attention. As inference demand accelerated, the share of compute allocated to training had steadily declined. Recently, however, training's share has risen sharply again. Despite the inference boom, Anthropic appears to be shifting more of its compute allocation back toward training. That doesn't mean inference demand is falling. Both training and inference can expand as total compute capacity grows. The AI model race is far from over, and the need for massive infrastructure investment in next-generation training remains. Gerstner's perspective on Jensen Huang was equally interesting. He believes NVIDIA's board should not have rushed to judgment without establishing all the facts. Drawing on decades of investing experience, he emphasized the strengths of founder-led technology companies and appeared concerned about NVIDIA becoming a conventional corporate-led organization. I share that concern. NVIDIA is far more than a GPU company. It has expanded across AI infrastructure, networking, robotics, and quantum computing. Who can truly replace Jensen's vision and influence? AI infrastructure competition is still accelerating, yet the company at the center of it all is contemplating a future without its founder. Quite an ironic moment.

external_articles.title: GitHub - ivanfioravanti/mlx-d1-gestures: Webcam to hand gesture and facial expression with Liquid AI's d1-2B on Apple Silicon (mlx-vlm), zero tokens generated
external_articles.body:
Your webcam in, hand gesture and facial expression out, live, on a Mac.

d1-2B by Liquid AI is a decision model, not a chat model. Each webcam frame gets four typed questions (which gesture? which expression? where is the hand? where is the face?), and one forward pass answers all of them with calibrated probabilities. It generates 0 tokens : all the work is prefill. On an M5 Max that is about 70 ms and ~600 input tokens per frame, roughly 14 decisions a second. It runs through mlx-vlm .

Everything stays on your Mac: the page and the model are served from 127.0.0.1 , and no frame is uploaded anywhere.

It starts decide.py and opens http://127.0.0.1:8049 once the model is ready (Ctrl-C stops it). Press Start camera and allow it. The first run downloads the model (2.2 GB). Prefer it by hand? uv run decide.py , then open the page.

Try thumbs up, thumbs down, OK, peace, open palm, pointing, a fist. Then smile, look sad or surprised, or keep a neutral face. Hold each one still for a second, close to the camera.

To ask something else, edit QUESTIONS in decide.py . A choice question answers with one key of its criteria , and a box question answers with where the thing is. If you add or rename a key, also add its label to HAND / FACE in index.html .

The page has a three-way selector: MLX (the default), Core AI GPU and Core AI Neural Engine . The two Core AI backends run d1-2B exported from the PyTorch weights to Core AI as one fixed-shape function: the 640×360 frame and the prompt for QUESTIONS in, the answer logits out. The questions are an input, not part of the model. A small Swift worker runs it; decide.py starts it on first use and keeps it warm. POST /run?backend=mlx|coreai-gpu|coreai-ane picks the backend per request, and GET /status says which are available. Without the worker below, MLX works as before, and the Core AI buttons are disabled with the reason.

The two models are on Hugging Face, ivanfioravanti/d1-2B-gestures-CoreAI (LFM Open License v1.0, converted from LiquidAI/d1-2B ). decide.py downloads each one the first time you select it (3.1 GB each, then cached), plus d1's input embedding table (500 MB), which it needs to build the prompt. All you build is the worker (Xcode 27):

To export the models yourself instead (uv, and a checkout of apple/coreai-models at ~/github/coreai-models ), then run with D1_COREAI_DIR=coreai/out :

The questions are not baked into the export. decide.py builds the prompt for QUESTIONS when it starts, so after editing them the Core AI backends answer the new questions with the same models. The export is padded to fixed sizes: up to 640 tokens of prompt (the image is 220 of them; today's questions use 578), 16 answer positions (a choice takes 1, a box 5) and 1152 readout tokens. Questions that don't fit make the Core AI backends refuse with the sizes, and MLX still works. export_gpu.py / export_ane.py trace the function with the prompt from coreai/questions.py , which only sets the shapes. The Core AI export is traced at one shape, 16:9 (640×360, what the page sends from a 16:9 webcam). Core AI centre-crops other frame shapes, such as a 4:3 webcam or a square photo, to 16:9 before the model sees them. Its boxes are mapped back onto the whole frame, but anything outside the crop is invisible to it: a face cut by the crop gets a box that stops at the crop's edge. MLX takes every shape as it is.

Measured on an M5 Max (macOS 27.3) with the same frame. Each decision is timed from the picture to the answers (preprocessing, model, readout), median of 30 after 5 warm-ups. Model time is measured inside the Swift worker:

The Neural Engine build runs the whole graph on the Neural Engine. Its compiled plan is marked mps.fullyPlacedOnANE and mps.noGPUActivity . It is about 3× slower than the GPU for this 2B model but draws far less power: about 3.2 J per decision against 6.0 J for Core AI GPU and 8.4 J for MLX (whole Mac, above idle). Each MLP is computed in 8 chunks of its hidden channels, which made the Neural Engine 1.4× faster (from 236 to 171 ms); int8 weights did not help it. The first switch to it compiles for the Neural Engine, which takes about a minute once, and the request waits. After that, Core AI's cache makes it start in under a second. Its one miss on the test frames is a uniform mid-gray frame: same answers, but a probability off by 0.051, against the 0.05 tolerance. Every real frame matches. To match the GPU's numbers, the Neural Engine export needed exact rescalings of its weights: the Neural Engine loses precision on very small activations and its sigmoid is coarse. The model card lists every change. Int8 weights halve the size, but they bring no speedup on the GPU and don't keep parity on the Neural Engine, so they are not used.

With mactop installed ( brew install mactop ), two charts under the video show the last 60 s of the Mac's CPU, GPU and Neural Engine load and its power draw, one sample a second, camera on or off, with a mark at each backend switch. Stop metrics pauses them, and decide.py stops mactop a few seconds later. The figures cover the whole Mac, not just d1: macOS camera effects such as backgrounds also run on the Neural Engine, so turn them off in Control Center → Video Effects before comparing backends. Even with them off, an open camera keeps macOS camera processing busy on the Neural Engine, so for a clean comparison press Load video and pick a local movie instead: the page plays it (it never leaves the browser, only its frames go to decide.py ) and the camera stays closed. On an M5 Max the Neural Engine runs at 100% busy and about 35 W for the whole Mac, while either GPU backend draws about 130 W.

The model looks at one still frame at a time, so it sees poses, not movements: a wave or a nod would need a short clip. Subtle expressions are harder to read, so exaggerate them.

items.title: https://t.co/CYB0vLZOxi TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/17/26 The window brought the first official government account of the Megaspeed investigation.
items.body: https://t.co/CYB0vLZOxi TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/17/26 The window brought the first official government account of the Megaspeed investigation. The Commerce and Justice Departments issued a joint statement setting out their timeline and putting the Justice Department in the lead on the criminal investigation, while making no allegation against Nvidia or Jensen Huang and saying nothing on the Entity List question. On the return question, reporting now has the board not considering bringing Huang back, the opposite direction from the comeback reporting in the record. President Trump and Vice President Vance both cast doubt on the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. In the Senate, the Commerce Committee's ranking member put four alleged export control failures in writing to Secretary Lutnick, and a Republican senator introduced a bill to force a listing decision on Megaspeed within 30 days. The shareholder case against Nvidia and Huang widened by amended complaint. THE GOVERNMENT SPEAKS • On November 16, 2026, the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation, posted by the Commerce Department's official account and issued expressly to address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting. The statement was read in full from the official post and verified word for word against a verbatim carriage and against Reuters reporting of the same statement. • The official timeline: after identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no sell list. • Also in June 2025, Bureau of Industry and Security agents, together with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person end-use check at Megaspeed and interviewed chief executive Alice Huang. Following that enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed. • The departments state they will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred, credit Secretary Lutnick's Commerce Department and Attorney General Blanche's Justice Department, and cite seventeen defendants charged across six semiconductor smuggling investigations under the Trump administration. • The statement makes no allegation against Nvidia or Jensen Huang, and it does not address the Entity List question. It is the first official Commerce or Justice Department statement in the record on the investigation's posture and timeline. Its account of the Commerce probe does not use the word suspended, which is the word Senator Cantwell's letter, filed in this same window, uses for what happened when the Justice Department took the criminal investigation. THE BOARD IS NOT DISCUSSING A RETURN • CNBC reported on Monday, November 16, 2026 that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as chief executive and is not in discussions to do so, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity. The Washington Post, citing a person familiar with the board's thinking, and the Financial Times reported the same position the same day. • CNBC reported the board is focused on its investigation into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets, an investigation CNBC reported is led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton. • This is reporting, not a board act: the board itself issued no statement, and Nvidia has not commented on whether a return would be considered. No prior claim in the record has the board, through any channel, ruling a return out of discussion. • CNBC also reported that the Stand with Jensen petition had drawn about 180,000 signatures, with public support from Elon Musk, Garry Tan and Tim Sweeney, and that Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. TRUMP AND VANCE ON ALICE HUANG • President Trump's full South Lawn departure gaggle on Monday, November 16, 2026 went materially beyond the reinstatement clip already in the record. Asked whether he trusted the intelligence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and whether Secretary Rubio had told him she was, Trump answered verbatim: "I don't know that she's a Chinese spy. I told Stephen [Smith] that... I haven't heard that. I don't know she's a spy... Nobody's proven that. She may not be a spy" and "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all." That portion was verified firsthand against the downloaded clip, transcribed in full. • On national security, Trump said: "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before." • On the Megaspeed Entity List delay, Trump said Secretary Lutnick "might have delayed it, but he was doing that because if you didn't delay it, if you didn't do something, you could have a blow up with China," adding "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it." No prior claim records Trump publicly attributing the delay to avoiding a blow up with China. • On the Bessent and Lutnick rift, Trump said: "One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China... They both are acceptable but they are different views." Asked whether he still has confidence in Lutnick, he answered "Yeah, I do," with no plans to replace him. Asked whether he would raise the spy allegations with Xi Jinping, he answered "I may." • Vice President JD Vance, on The Ingraham Angle aired Monday evening, November 16, 2026, said of Alice Huang, verbatim and verified firsthand against the program's clip: "I don't know, and he doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," explaining that "this intelligence always points in different directions" and that "because the intelligence disagrees with itself" there is "a lack of clarity about it." • Vance said whether she was a spy "actually is not the main issue. The main issue is we need to reindustrialize the country and protect our critical technology and our critical infrastructure," and attacked Democrats for using "this very salacious story about Jensen [Huang] and this mistress" to accuse Trump of being soft on China. No prior claim records Vance speaking on the matter, or an administration statement that the intelligence on Alice Huang is internally contradictory. CANTWELL PUTS IT IN WRITING • Senator Maria Cantwell, ranking member of the Senate Commerce Committee, sent a letter dated November 15, 2026 to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, published in full by the committee on November 16, 2026 and read in full. Reuters reported the letter the same day; a Lutnick spokesperson declined to comment. • The letter charges that Lutnick's failure to use his Export Control Reform Act authorities "has undermined America's national security." Its four specific failures are the senator's assertions, recorded here as allegations, not as verified facts. • First, Commerce has refused to close the remote access loophole, leaving PRC companies training advanced models on United States chips abroad. Second, Commerce resisted Treasury, State and Defense efforts to restrict Megaspeed despite officials urging restriction beginning in fall 2025 and a classified warning to Lutnick in May 2026. • Third, Commerce suspended its administrative investigation of Megaspeed after Nvidia's general counsel reportedly contacted investigators in August 2025, apparently with Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler's permission, when the Justice Department requested transfer for criminal investigation, and did so without restricting Megaspeed. Fourth, Commerce twice suspended the September 2025 Bureau of Industry and Security rule extending export restrictions to majority-owned subsidiaries of restricted companies, the suspension now running through January 10, 2027. • The letter also raises financial conflicts: Cantor Fitzgerald, controlled by Lutnick's sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at his nomination, and the administration's 25 percent fee on certain Nvidia chip sales to China creates, in the letter's words, "a perverse financial incentive." It closes: "America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls." • No prior claim in the record mentions Cantwell. The letter is the first Senate Commerce leadership document in the record. A BILL TO FORCE THE LISTING DECISION • Senator Pete Ricketts introduced the MEGA Act on November 17, 2026, per his office's press release of the same date, read in full. The legislation would require the Department of Commerce to decide within 30 days whether to add Megaspeed to the United States Entity List. Ricketts supports adding the company to the Entity List, and said verbatim: "Megaspeed's ties to Communist China demand action. We cannot delay any longer." • As released, the bill would immediately require export licenses for transactions involving Megaspeed, with a presumption of denial, and authorize restrictions on related companies, with interim restrictions in place until the final decision takes effect. It would permit 30-day extensions if the Attorney General certifies the deadline would jeopardize an ongoing federal criminal investigation or prosecution, and would require Commerce to explain its decision to Congress. • The release's backdrop notes that State, War, Energy and Treasury have supported adding Megaspeed per recent reporting, that Commerce has not designated the company, and that Commerce's November 16 remote access restrictions do not resolve Megaspeed's status. • No prior claim in the record mentions Ricketts or any legislation directed at Megaspeed's listing. This is the first bill in the record that would set a statutory 30-day decision deadline on the Entity List question at the center of the Bessent and Lutnick dispute. THE SHAREHOLDER CASE WIDENS • An amended complaint was filed on November 13, 2026 in Kistenmacher v. NVIDIA Corporation and Jen-Hsun Huang, Case No. 5:26-cv-13448 in the Northern District of California, and is now the operative complaint. The amended complaint itself was not read firsthand; its filing, date and terms are carried identically by Open Class Actions and Hagens Berman. • The amended complaint widened the proposed class period to December 19, 2024 through November 12, 2026, from October 9, 2025 through November 8, 2026 in the original November 9, 2026 complaint. The case brings claims under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act, alleging Nvidia's public statements about Megaspeed were misleading, is assigned to Judge Charles R. Breyer, and carries a lead plaintiff deadline of January 8, 2027. • The allegations are unproven, no class has been certified, and Nvidia has not responded in court. THE CHECKPOINTS • November 17, 2026: Nvidia earnings after the close, Kress's first earnings call, and the Warren and Coons records preservation confirmation is due. • November 18, 2026: the closed-door briefing. • November 24, 2026: Bennet's answers due. • About November 25, 2026: Bessent's 10-day deadline for answers from Nvidia's board and outside counsel. • December 1, 2026: Huang's closed-door transcribed interview track, date not locked, and the House Foreign Affairs Democrats' answers due. • December 2, 2026: Teter's requested closed-door transcribed interview. • December 3, 2026: Scott's requested public Senate Banking hearing with Huang, and the Foreign Affairs hearing with Under Secretary Kessler. • December 10, 2026

external_articles.title: Jensengate | Atlas Peak Research
external_articles.body:
The fall of Jensen Huang at Nvidia, tracked in twelve-hour editions: the newest edition in full at the top, and every earlier edition in the archive below.

TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/17/26

The window brought the first official government account of the Megaspeed investigation. The Commerce and Justice Departments issued a joint statement setting out their timeline and putting the Justice Department in the lead on the criminal investigation, while making no allegation against Nvidia or Jensen Huang and saying nothing on the Entity List question. On the return question, reporting now has the board not considering bringing Huang back, the opposite direction from the comeback reporting in the record. President Trump and Vice President Vance both cast doubt on the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. In the Senate, the Commerce Committee's ranking member put four alleged export control failures in writing to Secretary Lutnick, and a Republican senator introduced a bill to force a listing decision on Megaspeed within 30 days. The shareholder case against Nvidia and Huang widened by amended complaint.

In this window the first government act in the case landed. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule closing the remote access channel at the center of the Megaspeed business model, and imposed a new destination license requirement covering Singapore and Malaysia, Megaspeed's two operating jurisdictions. The Straits Times reported the first known enforcement action in Indonesia linked to the case, a police search of Megaspeed's Indonesian subsidiary that found empty server racks and no chips. President Trump publicly welcomed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as chief executive, in the opposite direction from his Treasury secretary's push for an outside chief executive.

In this window the succession fight split in public on the same Sunday shows that moved the congressional track. Jensen Huang has agreed to a closed-door interview with the three House committees, with no subpoena needed and the date still being discussed. A briefed Gang of Eight member said on the record that the intelligence community does not know whether Alice Huang was a witting asset. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent directed the board toward an outside chief executive and set it a 10-day deadline to answer on export-compliance culture, while the Financial Times reported Huang himself is discussing a comeback, with an ally war room lobbying for his return.

In this window the channel record widened again: the Wall Street Journal reported records showing Megaspeed arranged to send nearly $12 billion of top Nvidia chips to companies in China, a fifth chip figure with its own window, and reported an unwritten Nvidia rule capping partners' Chinese customers and a new channel node, Aolani Cloud. Megaspeed answered publicly for the first time on Alice Huang, saying she left the company effective August 30, 2025 and that it has retained outside counsel for an internal investigation. The Washington Post reported Huang is quietly helping pick his own successor, and Elon Musk said many of Nvidia's supply deals were a handshake with Huang personally.

In this window the fight over the classified memo at the center of the case widened: the Washington Post reported the memo was Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recasting of a CIA report in more assertive terms, and CNN reported the CIA is not yet convinced the intercepts prove Alice Huang knowingly funneled information to Beijing. The Financial Times reported Nvidia carries directors and officers insurance that protects its directors personally and not the company, filings show a director sold about $946.6 million of stock in the weeks before the board inquiry opened, and Reuters reported Chinese AI firms are racing to reserve Nvidia powered capacity outside China before the remote rental loophole closes. South Korea said Nvidia has reconfirmed its 260,000 GPU supply plan after the resignation, Bill Ackman defended Huang on presumption of innocence grounds, and the first Sunday show booking for a case chair was announced for tomorrow.

Overnight, Reuters reported that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's own general counsel and chief marketing officer in writing that his interactions with Alice Huang and Megaspeed were standard business dealings, the House chairs' 8 p.m. deadline for his written acceptance of the December 1 interview passed with nothing public, and a filings-based reconstruction put $5,353 million of Nvidia's formerly Singapore-billed revenue with China and Hong Kong headquartered buyers. Super Micro denied on the record that Megaspeed was ever its customer, a sitting administration official argued Huang should have been warned the way a congressman once was, and the street kept repricing the overhang: HSBC cut its target by more than half, and a billionaire holder said he will make no further investment in Nvidia without Huang.

Today the fight over the Megaspeed Entity List delay became an open cabinet split, the Commerce Secretary's own tenure came into question, Reuters documented the scale of Chinese AI projects built around restricted Nvidia chips, and the succession search moved in public for the first time: the board was reported to have approached an external candidate, then issued its first statement calling candidate speculation premature, while two major holders asked the board to slow the process down and keep Jensen Huang's return on the table. The 8 p.m. deadline for Huang's written acceptance of the December 1 interview passed with nothing public.

THE SUCCESSION SEARCH MOVES, THEN THE BOARD PUSHES BACK

Overnight, the House turned its request to Jensen Huang into an ultimatum with a deadline tonight, the Senate Banking subpoena threat was verified from the letter itself and shown to run to Huang only, Bloomberg published the first account of how the admission and the resignation decision actually happened, Malaysia opened its own official inquiry into the Megaspeed channel while its prime minister said there is no indication so far that chips were exported from Malaysia, and CNN's reporting reframed the Alice Huang spy question toward recruitment after access.

The first full day after Jensen Huang's resignation widened the case on every front at once. Huang agreed to testify before Congress, the Senate Banking Committee requested dated public hearings for Huang and for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, the tax committees opened their own investigation with a records preservation demand, the Justice Department spoke on the record for the first time, Singapore published its full account of the Alice Huang investigation, and the channel record added two new end points, DeepSeek and Huawei.

THE TAX COMMITTEES OPEN AN INVESTIGATION

The case resolved overnight. Nvidia announced this morning that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately, ending the board process that had built through the night: Semafor had reported some directors favored CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, and Kress is the interim appointment in the release. The night also deepened the record behind the case, with the Wall Street Journal's account of the husband who introduced Huang to Alice Huang, Congress turning its fire on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Megaspeed's first public statement, and the analyst downgrade wave broadening before the announcement landed.

In twelve hours the case moved from congressional pressure to the boardroom. The New York Times reported a second extramarital relationship, this one with a direct report. The Wall Street Journal reported the board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang, and Bloomberg reported a succession search is under way. The committees' 5 PM deadline for his answer on the November 18 briefing passed with no acceptance or alternative date reported, and the desk raised its exit estimate in this window.

Atlas Peak Research. Compiled from public reporting, company statements, and congressional and court records. Each edition covers twelve hours of the case and appears here in full.

Updated 11/17/26 10:11 AM ET · 11 editions

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.body: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space , because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

items.body: $BE has a bigger advantage in BTM power than most you realize. Gas engines and turbines are often cheaper, but good luck getting them permitted next to residential areas. Noise and NOx emissions are becoming real problems for developers. Look at $NBIS Vineland (it's just example Bloom's fuel cells solve much of that. No combustion, very low NOx, significantly less noise, and 50%+ electrical efficiency. And the Brookfield deal makes this even more interesting. Up to $25B in project financing. Brookfield can fund the upfront CAPEX while customers pay for electricity under long-term agreements. So Bloom doesn't necessarily need to win on $/MWh. If your gas project takes another 18 months to get approved while Bloom can get you powered sooner, how much is that time worth when you have hundreds of millions in GPUs sitting idle? That's where I think $BE has a real edge. Not everywhere, but in exactly the locations where getting power is becoming the hardest part of building an AI data center.

In case you missed it: 📊 Earnings Visuals (10/2026) 🤖 How Anthropic Makes Money 💻 PRO: Microsoft Azure Hits 48% 🚨 NVIDIA: Jensen Huang Resigns Subscribe now It’s 13F season again! Every quarter, funds managing over $100 million must disclose their portfolios, offering a rare glimpse into the minds of elite investors. The latest 13F filings capture portfolios as of September 30. Of course, a lot has happened since then. At the end of Q3, the AI infrastructure boom was still in full swing. Hyperscalers were pouring billions into data centers, semiconductor stocks were riding a wave of demand, and investors were looking for the next beneficiaries across the supply chain. Fast-forward six weeks, and the picture looks very different. The Democrats swept the midterm elections, voters pushed back against new data centers, and NVIDIA lost its longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, in a stunning leadership shakeup. Meanwhile, the AI trade has suffered a sharp selloff. Concerns about circular financing, the returns on massive AI investments, and persistently high inflation have weighed on valuations. So where were the world’s leading investors putting their money before the turmoil? Were they still piling into AI infrastructure, taking profits, or finding opportunities elsewhere? Let’s find out. Today at a glance: Hedge funds’ strategies Top buys and top holdings in Q3 Fund picks that were not on your bingo card Implications for individual investors 📊 Black Friday: PRO is 40% off for life Get our weekly PRO coverage of the biggest market leaders, with timely earnings breakdowns, KPI tracking, and visuals that help connect the dots. For Black Friday, unlock PRO at $299/year instead of $499/year, and keep that price for as long as your subscription remains active. But don’t wait! The offer ends on Sunday. Go PRO 40% Off Before we dive into 13Fs, a quick reminder: blindly copying hedge fund trades is a terrible strategy. Investing is like shooting 3-pointers. Even Steph Curry, the greatest shooter ever, misses more than half the time. No outcomes are guaranteed, even for the pros. Your behavior matters more than your portfolio. As Peter Lynch said, “Know what you own and why you own it.” Conviction is what helps you hold through volatility. And conviction comes from doing your own work, not borrowing someone else’s. As Ian Cassel puts it: “You can borrow someone else’s stock ideas but you can’t borrow their conviction. […] Do the work so you know when to sell. Do the work so you can hold. Do the work so you can stand alone.” Some limitations of 13F filings: Omit short positions and cash reserves. Offer a partial view , leaving out smaller funds. Exclude many non-US equities , bonds, and commodities. Can be dated , as filings are due up to 45 days after quarter-end. With all this said, let’s see what top funds were buying and holding in Q3. 1. Hedge funds’ strategies Hedge funds are financial powerhouses known for flexible, aggressive strategies designed to beat the market. Here’s what typically shapes their moves: Market conditions : Long in bull markets, defensive in bear markets. Sector trends : Shifts in regulation or consumer behavior steer capital. Fundamentals : Strong earnings, free cash flow, and leadership matter. Macro factors : Rates, inflation, and geopolitics influence positioning. Quant models : Some lean on proprietary algorithms to find an edge. Risk management : Diversification, hedging, and position sizing. Investor sentiment : Fear and greed create mispriced opportunities. Still, it doesn’t always work out. The Global X Guru ETF (GURU), designed to track top hedge fund holdings, has underperformed the S&P 500 since its inception in 2012. And that comparison still leaves out the classic hedge fund fee drag. Source: Fiscal.ai And those fees matter. The classic “2 and 20” model (2% of assets + 20% of gains) can significantly reduce returns. It’s no wonder that many individual investors are opting for simpler, lower-cost strategies. 2. Top holdings and top buys in Q3 Our partners at Fiscal.ai gather the data on Super Investors and visualize their portfolios for you. Meta saw the biggest jump, rising from three to nine appearances. Microsoft also gained ground, moving from one to three. Meanwhile, Alphabet fell from eight to four, while NVIDIA held steady at five. Apple remains absent from the top-five holdings, while Tesla appears at Altimeter. Of course, these rankings reflect both portfolio decisions and stock-price movements. A company dropping out of a fund’s top five doesn’t necessarily mean the manager sold shares. items.body: Had fun writing this. Feel free to drop comments, thoughts, corrections, etc Note that I'd refrained from writing about MegaSpeed / SpeedMatrix, and other speculations (e.g. on YTL) The three takeaways from the post: 1. Malaysia's AI data center space is getting very crowded, especially in Johor 2. Demand for AI compute, infrastructure, and powered shells from Chinese customers, anchored by tech giants, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, as well as adjacents such as Bitdeer, has been the key growth driver behind the rapid AI data center buildout in Malaysia 3. Stranded capacity and/or pipeline growth risk is very real, with the latest rules announced by the US BIS, to be effective immediately once they are officially published on the Federal Register on Nov 19 (Thursday) Questions that we should ask: 1. Will the Chinese customers stay, or leave? 2. For the capacity slack (if any), will there be replacement demand, and from who? How much AI compute does Malaysia need for themselves (from their enterprises, government and sovereign AI initiatives)? Will we see demand from the West, particularly the US where data center approvals and new starts are expected to slow with the new Congress setup? 3. How much of the planned capacity (including those currently under construction, approved but not started) will eventually be completed, energized and ready for service (RFS)? 4. Will there be changes to hardware/system configurations at the existing facilities, and those in the pipeline? For the Chinese customers who choose to stay, will they bring in Chinese AI hardware? What happens to the US AI hardware already deployed, in transit, and / or committed?

items.body: $LITE $COHR $AAOI $SIVE $CRDO Pre-Market is FLYING. Do you understand why this news is so BULLISH for the optical stack? Trump admin is pressing ahead with the ban on new Chinese optical transceivers for US AI data centers despite heavy pushback from $AMZN $GOOGL $META. Chinese players currently control ~2/3 of the global market. The ban is driven by national security concerns (potential backdoors, data theft, service disruption) and is overriding the hyperscalers’ preference for cheaper/faster Chinese supply. This forces a direct transfer of market share, pricing power and multi-year visibility to Western suppliers that make the lasers, components and modules used inside AI data centers. > $LITE: High-performance lasers (the core light source). > $COHR: Full photonics platform + next-gen optical solutions. > $AAOI: Pure-play high-speed transceiver modules (800G/1.6T). > $SIVE: Micro-cap InP laser pure-play (highest asymmetry). > $CRDO: Optical DSPs + silicon photonics + its own modules. If China loses the ability to supply the critical path of AI interconnect. Western players get the volume and the margin. Position for the decoupling. NFA.

items.title: This is one of the most challenging IG parts about the aggregate ROIC debate… Thinking out loud, the funding pool can clearly extend beyond the labs. The ROIC challenge is isolatin
items.body: This is one of the most challenging IG parts about the aggregate ROIC debate… Thinking out loud, the funding pool can clearly extend beyond the labs. The ROIC challenge is isolating how much of that growth AI created versus what these already enormous businesses would have generated anyway. Ads are unique too since they offer particularly attractive returns: better monetization of existing traffic can carry high incremental margins. A dollar of ad growth and a dollar of lab/cloud revenue can contribute very different amounts of profit. The harder aggregate issue is substitution. AI could capture existing software and services spending while adding compute costs and capital intensity. Individual winners could do well while industry ROIC falls. Cost savings and protecting existing profits can justify investment, but we still need enough incremental profit to earn a return on the expanding capital base.

external_articles.title: 5th CSN Greece ICT Conference – Cyprus Shipping Events
external_articles.body:
The 5th CSN Greece ICT Conference, titled “Intelligent Skies, Secure Seas: The AI Impact on ICT”, will take place on 19th November 2026 at the Ploes Floating Venue in Athens.

The conference is placed under the auspices of AMMITEC and supported by the Hellenic Chamber of Shipping , the Propeller Club , HELMEPA , WIMA , Business Events Calendar and MASO Strategic .

Attendance is free of charge for all members of the supporting organisations. However, attendees are encouraged to contribute to the charity foundation supported by the conference , with the option to donate indicated during registration.

Join us to navigate the crossroads of innovation and security and to chart a smarter, safer course for maritime’s digital evolution.

Registration and Welcome Coffee Sponsored by MARPOINT

Note from the organiser Adonis Violaris, Managing Director – CSN

Welcome Address from the Chairman of the Conference Dr. Matthew Maheras, President, AMMITEC, and Chief Information Officer, Metrostar Management Corp.

Keynote Speech Demetris Skourides, Chairman – Research Innovation Foundation Cyprus

We are well past the days of treating ship-to-shore connectivity as a luxury; today’s vessel is an “always-on” operational node. In this session, we will tackle the bandwidth battles head-on, examining how the convergence of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations and maritime 5G is fundamentally altering fleet management.

However, we need to separate what is actually working at sea from what looks good in a brochure. To achieve this, the session will feature our MythBusters format. We have all sat through enough polished sales presentations—this rapid-fire debate will strip away the marketing hype to establish the technical reality of modern satellite communications. We will focus purely on what delivers tangible ROI, what ensures reliable redundancy, and what is merely industry noise.

Setting the Scene: Connectivity as an Operational Reality Dimitris Pavlides, IT Manager – Stealth Maritime

Panel discussion: “MythBusters: SatComs Reality Check”

Moderator: Dimitris Pavlides, IT Manager – Stealth Maritime

Panelists: – Apostolos Giannetsos, ICT Manager – Cyprus Sea Lines – Nikolas Sarantos, ICT Manager – Seahawk Group – Thanos Servos, IT Manager – Seaven – Yiannis Sofianidis, IT Director/CISO – AM Nomikos TWMA SA. – Ilias Vlachogiannis, Head of Fleet ICT – Minerva Marine Inc.

For too long, the maritime sector has treated cybersecurity as a mere compliance exercise. With ships now operating as highly connected, floating data centres, a tick-box approach is no longer fit for purpose. This session focuses on the necessary shift from basic compliance to real-time, dynamic resilience, exploring how we can build robust “human firewall” strategies from the boardroom to the engine room.

To drive this home, we are moving away from the standard slide decks on malware and introducing The War Room . This is a live, audience-driven cyber-attack simulation on a vessel at sea. We will put attendees in the hot seat, forcing them to make critical operational and commercial decisions under pressure. It is designed to stress-test our collective incident response and show exactly what happens when the screens go dark.

Securing the Connected Ecosystem Fotis Tsitsirigkos , Maritime Technology Advisor – FTTCS

Panel discussion: “The War Room: Live Cyber-Attack Simulation on a Vessel”

Moderator: Fotis Tsitsirigkos , Maritime Technology Advisor – FTTCS

Panelists: – Dimitris Perdikaris, Company Security Officer / DPA – Plutofylax Shipping – Manolis Papadakis, CIO/CISO – Dynagas – Ioannis Pantazopoulos, Regional Manager Greece, Cyprus and Turkey – Division Air France, KLM and Delta Air Lines – Demetris Skourides, Chairman – Research Innovation Foundation Cyprus – Kyriakos Mahos, HSQE Director, DPA & CSO – Levante Ferries

AI is actively moving from a conceptual talking point to an operational tool, redefining route optimisation, predictive maintenance, and threat detection. Yet, the introduction of machine intelligence inevitably creates friction with traditional human maritime expertise. We need to understand the new synergy required between the algorithm and the crew.

We will confront these complex dynamics directly through The AI Courtroom . This mock trial will tackle the difficult questions that most panels avoid: the ethics, commercial liability, and legal reality of autonomous and AI-assisted technology. If an AI-optimised system recommends a route that results in an incident, where does the liability lie? Is the industry truly ready to let the algorithm take the wheel?

The Synergy and Friction Between Human and Machine Intelligence Konstantinos Bachxevanis, Solicitor E&W/ Piraeus Bar Lawyer/ Master Mariner – BAX LAW

Panel discussion: “The AI Courtroom: A Mock Trial”

Moderator: Konstantinos Bachxevanis, Solicitor E&W/ Piraeus Bar Lawyer/ Master Mariner – BAX LAW

Panelists: – Konstantinos Stais, Head of ICT & Security – Delia Tankers – Capt. Athanasios Skiadas, Safety Manager/DPA/CSO – Calypso Marine – Capt.George Papanelopoulos, Head of Vetting, Training & Development Dept. – Cyprus Sea Lines Co Ltd – John N. Faraclas, Co-Founder – All About Shipping – George Karistinos, Business Development Manager – ABS Wavesight

This conference is curated for Maritime C-Suite, CIOs, CISOs, Fleet Managers, and Technical Superintendents. If you need to understand the ROI of connectivity, manage the liability of cyber risks, and future-proof your fleet against digital obsolescence, this is your arena.

Closing remarks from the chairman Dr. Matthew Maheras, President, AMMITEC, and Chief Information Officer, Metrostar Management Corp.

Thank you from the organisers Adonis Violaris, Managing Director – CSN

CIO - Metrostar Management / President - AMMITEC

Chairman - Research Innovation Foundation Cyprus

Company Security Officer / DPA – Plutofylax Shipping

If you have any questions we can answer it! Although we are here to hear you!
